questions.title: Deadlock Storm Under Load: Root Cause and Prevention
questions.prompt: Your OLTP system is throwing an increasing number of deadlock errors (1205) during peak hours, and the on-call team's current fix is just to retry the failed transaction. As the architect, walk through: what a deadlock actually is at the lock-manager level, why SQL Server resolves it by picking a victim, and the concrete, durable design changes you'd make to drive the deadlock rate toward zero rather than just making retries cheaper.
questions.modelAnswer: A deadlock is a circular wait: Transaction A holds a lock Transaction B needs, while B simultaneously holds a lock A needs, so neither can ever proceed without intervention. SQL Server's lock monitor periodically scans for exactly this cycle and, once found, picks a 'victim' to roll back automatically, based on which transaction is cheaper to undo (or an explicit DEADLOCK_PRIORITY setting), raising error 1205 to the victim's caller. Retrying the rolled-back transaction only treats the symptom — it does nothing to reduce how often the cycle forms in the first place. The durable fixes are architectural: (1) enforce a consistent access order to tables across every code path that touches them, since the single most common real-world cause is two transactions locking the same two tables in opposite order; (2) keep transactions as short as possible, moving validation and unrelated reads outside the BEGIN/COMMIT boundary so locks are held for the minimum necessary time; (3) review indexing so transactions acquire narrow row/page locks instead of escalating to page or table locks on large scans, which dramatically widens the blast radius of any single transaction; (4) consider READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT isolation, which removes most reader/writer blocking entirely via row versioning, at the cost of additional tempdb version-store overhead; (5) for cases where natural ordering genuinely can't be enforced, use sp_getapplock to serialize access explicitly. Before declaring any fix complete, capture an actual deadlock graph (via Extended Events' xml_deadlock_report) to confirm the real access pattern rather than guessing from symptoms.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the team, respectfully, that retrying is a band-aid, not a fix — it just hides the real cost of the problem. First I'd pull an actual deadlock graph, not just the error count, because I want to see exactly which two statements and which two resources are colliding before I propose anything. Nine times out of ten it comes down to two code paths touching the same tables in opposite order, so step one is standardizing access order across every stored procedure that touches those tables. Step two is auditing transaction length — anything that's validating data or doing unrelated reads inside the BEGIN/COMMIT boundary comes out. Then I look at whether lock escalation is widening the blast radius because of missing indexes, and only after that do I bring up snapshot isolation as a structural option, being upfront that it moves the cost into tempdb rather than eliminating it. I'd present this as 'here's the mechanism, here's the evidence, here's what actually gets the rate toward zero' rather than just 'add a try/catch and retry.'

Doesn't look at actual access order across stored procedures
Ignores lock escalation thresholds on large updates
Assumes deadlocks are a bug SQL Server should prevent rather than a resolvable mutual-wait
Never captures an actual deadlock graph (XML) before proposing a fix
keyPoints: Defines deadlock as a circular wait on locks, not a generic error
Explains SQL Server's victim-selection mechanism
Identifies inconsistent access order as the most common root cause
Proposes shortening transactions and reviewing indexing to reduce lock footprint
Considers snapshot isolation as an architectural lever, with its tradeoff (tempdb/version store)
Recommends instrumentation (deadlock graph / extended events) before declaring a fix

questions.title: Reporting Queries Are Blocking the Nightly Order Pipeline
questions.prompt: Business users running ad-hoc reports against the live OLTP database during business hours are intermittently blocking order-entry transactions, and vice versa. Compare the architectural options — read-committed snapshot isolation, a reporting replica, and query hints like NOLOCK — and recommend what you'd actually implement, including what you give up.
questions.modelAnswer: Under the default READ COMMITTED isolation level, readers take shared locks and writers take exclusive locks, so reports and order-entry transactions genuinely contend for the same locks on the same rows, causing exactly this symptom. NOLOCK (or READ UNCOMMITTED) removes that blocking by skipping locking entirely, but it allows dirty reads, can double-count or miss rows during a page split, and is unacceptable for anything a finance or operations team relies on for correctness — I would not recommend it as a general answer here. READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT (RCSI), enabled at the database level, gives readers a transactionally consistent versioned snapshot from tempdb's version store instead of taking shared locks, so reporting reads stop blocking writers and vice versa, with zero application code changes for ordinary SELECTs — the cost is additional tempdb space and I/O for the version store, and a small per-row overhead on writers. A reporting replica (an Always On readable secondary, log shipping, or replication) solves a different, broader problem: it isolates the reporting workload's CPU and I/O consumption from the OLTP instance entirely, not just lock contention, at the cost of replication lag and additional infrastructure to maintain. My recommendation: enable RCSI first as the fast, low-risk fix for the specific symptom described (lock contention), and treat a readable secondary as the real architectural answer once the reporting workload itself starts consuming OLTP compute/I/O capacity, not just locks. The two aren't mutually exclusive — a mature design often has both.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd separate this into two different problems that look the same from the outside: lock contention, and resource contention. For the immediate symptom — reports and order entry fighting over row locks — I'd recommend turning on read-committed snapshot isolation. It lets readers work off a versioned snapshot instead of taking shared locks, so the blocking just stops, and it needs no code changes. I'd be upfront that it's not free — it adds load to tempdb's version store — but that's a much safer tradeoff than reaching for NOLOCK, which I'd actually argue against here, because dirty reads on order data are a real correctness risk, not just a theoretical one. If the real issue turns out to be that reporting is also eating CPU and I/O the OLTP system needs, that's a different conversation — that's when I'd bring in a readable secondary, because RCSI doesn't give you more hardware, it just removes lock contention. I'd frame it to the client as 'quick structural fix now, workload separation as the next step if reporting keeps growing.'
commonMistakes: Recommends NOLOCK as a general-purpose fix without flagging dirty-read risk
Doesn't distinguish lock contention from resource (CPU/IO) contention
Treats RCSI as free, ignoring tempdb version-store cost
Proposes a replica without acknowledging replication lag implications for 'real-time' reports
keyPoints: Explains why READ COMMITTED causes reader/writer blocking
Evaluates NOLOCK and correctly rejects it for anything requiring correctness
Explains RCSI's row-versioning mechanism and its tempdb cost
Recommends a readable secondary/replica as the durable architecture for resource isolation
Distinguishes lock contention from compute contention

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the locking behavior causing the blocking
Evaluates NOLOCK and its risks accurately
Explains RCSI/snapshot isolation mechanism and cost
Recommends and justifies an appropriate architecture (replica vs RCSI)

questions.title: A Stored Procedure Is Recompiling Constantly Under Load
questions.prompt: A heavily-used stored procedure builds a large intermediate result set using a table variable, then joins it twice more inside the same procedure. Under load, you're seeing wildly inconsistent execution times and plan cache bloat. Diagnose why the table variable choice is likely the architectural root cause at this scale, and rewrite the approach.
questions.modelAnswer: Table variables historically carry no real statistics — on many compatibility levels the optimizer assumes roughly one row regardless of actual size — so when the intermediate set is genuinely large, the optimizer builds a plan sized for one row: an undersized memory grant and a join strategy that's wrong for the real row count. The inconsistent timing comes from actual row counts varying run to run while the cached plan was compiled against that wrong, fixed assumption, so some executions get lucky and others spill to disk or pick a bad join type. A #temp table, by contrast, gets real statistics maintained by SQL Server, letting the optimizer size the plan for the two downstream joins accurately. The tradeoff: a significant change in a temp table's row count can trigger a recompile — but that's a feature here, not a bug, since it means the plan adapts to actual data instead of staying wrong. The fix is to replace the DECLARE @T TABLE with a CREATE TABLE #T, optionally indexed if the joins warrant it, keeping the rest of the procedure's logic unchanged.
questions.professionalAnswer: What's happening here is that the optimizer doesn't have real numbers to work with. A table variable, on most compatibility levels, gets treated as roughly one row no matter how big it actually gets, so the plan built for it is sized for the wrong workload — that's exactly why the timing is inconsistent: the actual row count varies, but the plan doesn't adapt. My fix is to swap it for a #temp table, because SQL Server maintains real statistics on those, so the two downstream joins get a plan that's actually shaped for the data. I'll be upfront that this trades one problem for a different, much smaller one — a temp table can trigger a recompile when its row count shifts significantly — but I'd rather have an occasional recompile that produces a correct plan than a stable plan that's confidently wrong every time.
questions.example:
-- Before: table variable, optimizer assumes ~1 row
CREATE PROCEDURE dbo.GetRegionalSalesSummary
AS
BEGIN
    DECLARE @ActiveOrders TABLE (OrderID INT, CustomerID INT, Amount MONEY);
    INSERT INTO @ActiveOrders
    SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, Amount FROM dbo.Orders WHERE Status = 'Active';

    SELECT c.Region, SUM(a.Amount)
    FROM @ActiveOrders a
    JOIN dbo.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = a.CustomerID
    GROUP BY c.Region;
END
GO

-- After: temp table, real statistics, optionally indexed
CREATE PROCEDURE dbo.GetRegionalSalesSummary
AS
BEGIN
    CREATE TABLE #ActiveOrders (OrderID INT, CustomerID INT, Amount MONEY);
    CREATE INDEX IX_ActiveOrders_CustomerID ON #ActiveOrders (CustomerID);

    INSERT INTO #ActiveOrders
    SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, Amount FROM dbo.Orders WHERE Status = 'Active';

    SELECT c.Region, SUM(a.Amount)
    FROM #ActiveOrders a
    JOIN dbo.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = a.CustomerID
    GROUP BY c.Region;
END
GO
commonMistakes: Treats 'table variables are always faster' as a universal rule
Doesn't connect inconsistent timing to missing statistics on a large table variable
Recommends a CTE instead, missing that a CTE is re-evaluated/inlined and doesn't solve the cardinality problem either
Adds an index to the table variable via inline constraint without recognizing its limits
Ignores the recompile tradeoff when switching to a temp table
keyPoints: Explains the statistics difference between table variables and temp tables
Connects missing statistics to bad cardinality estimation and inconsistent plans at scale
Chooses #temp table over table variable or CTE for this specific large, multiply-joined scenario
Provides a correct before/after rewrite
Acknowledges the recompile tradeoff as acceptable here

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses missing statistics as the root cause
Chooses the right replacement structure with justification
Provides correct, working SQL example
Acknowledges tradeoffs (recompilation) honestly

questions.title: Licensing math for a mixed-consumption tenant
questions.prompt: Finance asks you to justify the Power BI licensing bill: 3,000 employees need to view dashboards, but only 200 of them ever build anything. Explain how per-user licenses (Free, Pro, PPU) interact with capacity assignment, and why the answer to 'what license does a viewer need' can't be given without also knowing where the content lives.
questions.modelAnswer: License and location are two independent variables that jointly determine access, and conflating them is the single most common licensing-cost mistake. A Free license lets someone build for themselves but never share or be shared with. A Pro license adds sharing and collaboration, but only with other Pro users, and only inside a shared (non-capacity) workspace. Premium Per User layers on most Premium features but, like Pro, only interoperates with other PPU users unless the content sits in a capacity. The moment content lives in a workspace assigned to a Premium or Fabric capacity, the rule changes completely: a Pro or PPU creator can share that content with a Free-license viewer, who consumes it without ever holding a paid per-user license. For 3,000 employees where only 200 build content, the economically correct model is: license the 200 builders as Pro (or PPU if they need PPU-only features like paginated reports or higher refresh limits without a capacity), put every workspace they publish to on a Fabric or Premium capacity, and leave the remaining 2,800 consumers on Free licenses — their access comes from the capacity, not from a per-user purchase. Skipping the capacity and instead licensing all 3,000 as Pro would cost dramatically more for identical end-user experience. The capacity's own cost (F64 or a Premium SKU) has to be weighed against that per-seat savings, but at 2,800 consumers the capacity almost always wins.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is a question I get asked by Finance more than by anyone technical, and the answer is: don't license the viewers, license the capacity. A Free license is genuinely free, but it's a dead end for sharing — Pro lets our 200 builders collaborate and publish, but Pro-to-Free sharing doesn't work in a plain shared workspace. The trick is capacity: once our builders' workspaces sit on a Fabric or Premium capacity, a Free-license employee can open and interact with that content with zero per-user cost. So my recommendation is 200 Pro licenses for the people actually building, one capacity SKU sized to our usage, and the other 2,800 people stay on Free. I'd also flag that if any of our builders need PPU-specific features — paginated reports, higher scheduled-refresh limits — without buying a capacity yet, PPU is the stopgap, but it only helps PPU-to-PPU sharing until we commit to a capacity. Bottom line: the capacity purchase is what turns 2,800 potential Pro licenses into zero.
commonMistakes: Assuming every viewer needs their own Pro license regardless of where content lives
Treating PPU as a cheaper substitute for a capacity when sharing with Free users is the actual goal
Forgetting that Pro-to-Pro sharing works without a capacity, but Pro-to-Free does not
Not weighing capacity SKU cost against the per-seat savings for a real recommendation
keyPoints: Free: personal use only, no sharing in or out
Pro: full sharing/collaboration, but only with other Pro users absent a capacity
PPU: Pro plus most Premium features, shareable only with other PPU users absent a capacity
Capacity (Premium/Fabric) is what lets a Free-license user consume shared content
Correct licensing model: license builders, capacity the workspace, leave consumers on Free

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly states what each license tier does and does not allow
Explains capacity's role in enabling Free-user consumption
Produces a concrete, cost-justified recommendation for the 3,000/200 split
Clarity suitable for a non-technical Finance stakeholder

questions.title: Separation of duties across workspace roles and apps
questions.prompt: An internal audit flags that too many people can both publish content and manage who sees it in your Power BI tenant. Design a separation-of-duties model using workspace roles (Admin/Member/Contributor/Viewer) and app audiences that gives publishers the ability to update content without giving them the ability to grant access, and explain where the boundaries actually sit.
questions.modelAnswer: The four workspace roles don't cleanly separate 'publish' from 'grant access' on their own — Member can publish content and add other members, and by default only Admins and Members can create or update an app, which conflates authorship with distribution authority. A real separation-of-duties model layers two decisions. First, restrict workspace Admin to a small platform-governance group (they alone can add/remove members, delete the workspace, change all settings); put day-to-day publishers in Contributor, not Member, so they can add, edit, and publish content but explicitly cannot manage who has workspace access — Contributor's defined limit is exactly 'can't manage who has access.' Second, move the actual access-granting decision out of the workspace entirely and into the app's Audience tab: a Contributor can be delegated the ability to create/update the app's content (a workspace setting exists to extend that permission to Contributors specifically), while the Audience membership itself — who is in the Sales audience versus the Leadership audience — stays owned by a smaller governance group, often the same people holding Admin. That split means a publisher can ship an updated report tomorrow without being able to add a new person to the Leadership audience, and the people who control audience membership never need day-to-day publish rights. One caveat to surface to audit: a direct link to content inside the app still works even for someone hidden from their audience's navigation — audience visibility is a navigation control, not a hard security boundary, so any row/column-level sensitivity still needs RLS/OLS underneath, not audience hiding alone.
questions.professionalAnswer: What I'd tell the audit team is: the workspace roles alone don't give you separation of duties for free — Member already lets someone publish and add new members, so if we just hand out Member broadly, we haven't actually separated anything. My fix is to drop day-to-day publishers to Contributor, which the platform already defines as 'can add, edit, and publish content, but can't manage who has access' — that's the separation we want, built in. Then I move the access-granting decision up a level, into the app's Audience tab, and I keep that owned by a small governance group, separate from the people actually shipping reports. If we want Contributors to be able to update the app's content without touching audience membership, there's a setting for that specifically — it's designed for exactly this split. The one thing I always flag to an audit team: hiding content from an audience is a navigation convenience, not a security control — anyone with a direct link still opens it — so if there's row-level sensitivity in play, that has to be RLS or OLS, not just audience visibility.
commonMistakes: Assuming Member already separates publish rights from access-granting rights
Treating audience hiding in an app as equivalent to real security
Not knowing the Contributor-can-update-app delegation setting exists
Letting the same small group hold both Admin and day-to-day publish duties, defeating the separation
keyPoints: Contributor can publish but explicitly can't manage workspace access
App Audience membership is a separate control point from workspace role
A delegation setting lets Contributors update app content without managing audiences
Audience hiding is navigation-only; direct links bypass it
Admin/governance group should stay distinct from day-to-day publishers

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly maps each workspace role's actual permission boundary
Proposes a workable separation-of-duties design using role + audience
Flags the direct-link/audience-hiding security caveat
Answer is actionable for an audit response, not just descriptive

questions.title: Choosing a storage mode for a governed semantic model
questions.prompt: You're designing the semantic model for a finance reporting platform that needs near-real-time accuracy on a small set of transactional tables but can tolerate a nightly refresh on large historical ones, and the source is entirely on-premises SQL Server. Compare Import, DirectQuery, Composite, and live connection to an existing Analysis Services model, and justify which one — or combination — you'd actually deploy, including the gateway and refresh implications.
questions.modelAnswer: Import copies data into memory and is fast to query but goes stale the moment the source changes, requiring scheduled or on-demand refresh. DirectQuery never copies data — every query passes through live to the source — which is always current but slower and fully dependent on the source and gateway being reachable at query time, not just at refresh time. Composite mixes both inside one model, letting individual tables pick whichever mode fits their own freshness/performance tradeoff. A live connection to an externally hosted Analysis Services model is a different axis entirely: it reuses an already-built model rather than importing or querying the organization's raw tables directly, which matters when a mature AS model already exists and duplicating that modeling effort would be wasteful — but Power BI can't mix Import/DirectQuery tables into a live-connected model the way Composite allows for its own tables. For this scenario — real-time transactional tables, tolerant historical ones, fully on-premises — Composite is the right call: the small transactional tables go DirectQuery so finance always sees current balances, and the large historical tables go Import so query performance on multi-year trend reports stays fast and doesn't hammer the source on every slicer click. Both modes against an on-premises source require a gateway (standard, for a shared multi-user setup) since neither DirectQuery nor Import can reach SQL Server directly from the cloud. The Import tables still need a refresh schedule (within the shared-capacity 8/day or Premium/Fabric 48/day limits), while the DirectQuery tables need no refresh schedule at all — but every query against them consumes gateway and source capacity in real time, so dashboard-heavy usage patterns against the DirectQuery tables need to be load-tested against the gateway, not just against Power BI's own limits.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame this as two separate questions that get conflated too often: 'how fresh does this table need to be' and 'do we already have a modeled source we should reuse.' For freshness, Composite is the answer here, not a compromise — DirectQuery the handful of transactional tables so finance never looks at stale balances, Import the large historical tables so trend reports stay fast and we're not re-querying years of data on every slicer click. Both paths need a gateway since we're fully on-prem; the Import side needs a refresh schedule and has to respect our capacity's daily refresh quota, while the DirectQuery side has no schedule but puts real-time load on that same gateway, so I'd load-test that before we ship it. The live-connection option is really a different conversation — that's for when there's already a mature Analysis Services model we don't want to rebuild, and it's an either/or against our own Composite modeling, not something we blend in. For this project specifically, since we're building the model ourselves against raw SQL Server tables, Composite is the right shape, not a live connection.
commonMistakes: Treating DirectQuery as refresh-free and therefore load-free, ignoring real-time gateway/source load
Assuming Composite can mix a live connection with Import/DirectQuery tables in the same model
Picking pure Import for everything and accepting staleness the business didn't agree to
Forgetting both Import and DirectQuery need a gateway for an on-premises source
keyPoints: Import: fast, needs scheduled/on-demand refresh, data copied into memory
DirectQuery: always current, slower, live source dependency, no refresh needed but real-time load
Composite: per-table choice of Import vs DirectQuery inside one model
Live connection: reuses an externally hosted AS model instead of building one, can't mix with Composite tables
On-premises source requires a gateway regardless of Import or DirectQuery

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Accurately compares all four modes and their tradeoffs
Produces a justified Composite design matching the stated freshness requirements
Correctly addresses gateway and refresh-quota implications
Avoids the common mistake of calling DirectQuery load-free

questions.title: RLS limits: rows, not columns, and the union rule
questions.prompt: A new analyst assigned to two RLS roles, 'West Sales' and 'National Accounts,' complains the dashboard shows data they weren't expecting to see — more than either role alone should allow. They also ask if RLS can hide the cost column from certain viewers. Using a real role expression, explain what's actually happening and what RLS structurally cannot do.
questions.modelAnswer: Both complaints trace back to the same structural fact: a role is a DAX filter expression applied to rows, nothing else, and multiple role memberships are additive, not intersective. With the two roles above, a user in both sees every row where Region = "West" OR AccountType = "National" — the union of what each role individually allows — not the intersection the analyst likely expected ('West AND National'). That's by design: RLS roles are meant to be composable grants, not AND-ed restrictions, so being added to a second role can only ever expand visibility, never narrow it. To get an intersection-style restriction, you'd need a single role whose DAX expression combines both conditions with AND, not two separate roles assigned together. On the second question — RLS cannot hide a column. If a user can see a row at all, under RLS they see every column of that row; restricting a column or a measure specifically (like hiding Cost while leaving Revenue visible) is object-level security (OLS), a distinct feature with its own configuration, not an extension of RLS. And critically, RLS only restricts users holding the workspace Viewer role — if the analyst has Contributor or above, no role assignment of any kind will restrict them, regardless of what the role's filter says.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk the analyst through it like this: being in two roles doesn't AND them together, it ORs them — you're now seeing West OR National, which is strictly more than either role shows alone, and that's intentional, because roles are meant to stack as additive grants. If what we actually want is 'West AND National accounts only,' that has to be one role with both conditions combined in its own filter expression, not two roles layered on top of each other. On the column question, I'd be direct: RLS can't do that, full stop — it filters which rows you see, and once you can see a row you see every column in it. Hiding a specific column like Cost is a different feature entirely, object-level security, and it needs to be configured separately. I'd also check one more thing before promising this will work at all: what workspace role is this analyst in? If they're a Contributor or higher, none of this RLS conversation matters, because RLS only binds Viewers.
commonMistakes: Assuming multiple RLS role memberships intersect rather than union
Believing RLS can restrict specific columns or measures
Not checking whether the affected user is actually a Viewer before debugging the role logic
Writing two separate roles when a single combined-condition role was needed
keyPoints: Multiple role membership is additive: union, not intersection
RLS filters rows only; column/measure restriction is OLS, a separate feature
RLS only applies to workspace Viewers — Admin/Member/Contributor are unaffected regardless of role assignment
A true AND-style restriction requires one role with a combined filter expression

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the union behavior of multiple roles
Correctly states RLS filters rows, not columns, and names OLS as the separate feature
Raises the Viewer-role-only applicability as a diagnostic step
Provides a correct fix for achieving an intersection restriction

questions.title: Parameter Sniffing: One Cached Plan, Two Very Different Row Counts
questions.prompt: A stored procedure filters orders by @CustomerID. For a customer with a handful of orders it returns in milliseconds; for your biggest customer with several million rows, the exact same procedure call times out. Nothing about the query changed. Explain what's actually happening at the plan-cache level, and lay out the durable fixes you'd choose between, including the tradeoffs of each.
questions.modelAnswer: This is parameter sniffing: when a stored procedure compiles, SQL Server peeks at the actual parameter value supplied on that first call and builds one cached execution plan optimized for that value's estimated row count, then reuses that same plan for every subsequent call regardless of what parameter comes in next. If the plan was compiled against a small customer, the optimizer chose a plan shaped for a small result set — likely nested loops with a lookup — and that same plan is catastrophic against a customer with millions of rows, where a hash or merge join with a full scan would have been far cheaper. The symptom isn't random; it's entirely a function of which value happened to compile the plan, which is why it looks like it 'used to work.' Durable fixes, in order of how I'd actually choose: (1) OPTION (RECOMPILE) on the statement forces a fresh, value-specific plan on every execution — correct for every call, but pays the compilation cost every single time, which is wasteful for a high-frequency procedure; (2) OPTION (OPTIMIZE FOR @CustomerID UNKNOWN) tells the optimizer to use the average-distribution estimate instead of sniffing any single value, which avoids the worst-case outlier plan but may make the common case slightly less optimal; (3) WITH RECOMPILE at the procedure level has the same cost profile as per-statement recompile but applies to the whole procedure; (4) query store plan forcing lets you pin a known-good plan once you've identified one that performs acceptably across the real distribution of parameter values, which is a strong operational fix but needs monitoring since data growth can eventually make the forced plan wrong too; (5) splitting the procedure into two paths (a small-customer branch and a large-customer branch, chosen by an IF before the query even runs) avoids a single plan ever having to serve both distributions, at the cost of more code to maintain. I'd pick based on call frequency and skew: for a rarely-called heavy procedure, RECOMPILE is cheap enough; for a hot-path procedure called thousands of times a minute, OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN or query store plan forcing is usually the right call, because paying a full recompile on every call would itself become the bottleneck.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it the same way I'd explain it to the team that paged me: the procedure didn't change, the data behind one parameter value did, and the plan cache is still serving a plan that was shaped for a tiny customer. SQL Server only looks at the parameter value once, on the first compile, and then it's locked in until something invalidates that plan. So the fix isn't 'optimize the query' — the query's fine — it's deciding how we want the optimizer to handle that skew going forward. For something called rarely, I'd just slap OPTION (RECOMPILE) on it and move on, because paying for a fresh plan every call is cheap compared to how rarely it runs. For something hot, I don't want to recompile constantly, so I'd reach for OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN first, which tells the optimizer to plan for the average case instead of gambling on whichever value shows up first — and if I need something more surgical, I'll go find a known-good plan and force it through Query Store, which I'll then keep an eye on, because a forced plan isn't a fix I set once and forget; the data keeps growing underneath it.
commonMistakes: Describes the symptom (it's slow for one customer) without naming the plan-cache mechanism causing it
Jumps straight to adding an index without addressing that a single cached plan is the root cause
Recommends OPTION (RECOMPILE) everywhere without weighing its per-call compilation cost on hot paths
Doesn't mention Query Store plan forcing as an operational option
Treats the fix as permanent without noting that data growth can make a forced or optimized-for plan wrong again later
keyPoints: Correctly explains that one parameter value's estimate shapes the cached plan for all future calls
Distinguishes RECOMPILE (per-call cost, always-correct plan) from OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN (average-case plan, no per-call cost)
Mentions Query Store plan forcing as a monitored, surgical fix
Considers call frequency and data skew when choosing between the options
Notes that any chosen fix needs to be revisited as data distribution changes over time

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the parameter-sniffing / plan-cache mechanism
Presents multiple durable fixes (RECOMPILE, OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN, Query Store forcing, branching)
Weighs the real tradeoffs (per-call cost vs. plan quality) rather than naming one fix blindly
Chooses between fixes based on call frequency / skew, not a one-size-fits-all answer

questions.title: Removing a Hardcoded Secret from a BI Staging Pipeline
questions.prompt: A Data Factory pipeline that stages data for the nightly Power BI refresh stores the source database password as a plaintext pipeline parameter, and a contractor who left the company six months ago still knows that password because it's visible in the pipeline JSON. Explain how you'd eliminate the stored secret using managed identity and/or Key Vault, and what you'd do about the fact that the contractor already has it.
questions.modelAnswer: The structural fix is to stop storing the credential at all. Where the target is Azure AD-integrated, I'd switch the linked service to authenticate with a system- or user-assigned managed identity, granting that identity only the minimum role it needs on the target data store, so no password ever exists in the pipeline definition. Where a literal credential genuinely can't be eliminated — a non-AAD database login, for instance — I'd store that secret once in Azure Key Vault and have the linked service reference it through a Key Vault-backed connection, so the pipeline JSON holds a vault reference, not a value. Neither of those changes matters, though, unless the actual exposed password gets rotated and the old login revoked outright — the whole point is that the contractor's knowledge of the old credential becomes worthless the moment it no longer works, not because they can't see it in JSON anymore. After the migration, the new access boundary is Key Vault and managed-identity role assignments, so I'd audit who has RBAC access to the vault and the identity's role scope, and I'd validate the new connection in Test before touching the production pipeline that feeds the nightly refresh.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd treat this as two separate problems that both need fixing, not one. The structural problem is that a password lives in plaintext in pipeline JSON at all — so wherever the target supports it, I'd move the linked service to a managed identity and grant it the least privilege it actually needs, and where that's not possible, I'd put the real secret in Key Vault once and have the linked service pull a reference to it instead of holding the value itself. But I'd be clear with the team that none of that actually solves the contractor problem by itself — what solves that is rotating the password and revoking the old login, full stop. The contractor knowing an old credential is meaningless once that credential doesn't work anymore. Once that's done, I'd shift my attention to the new boundary, which is now who has RBAC access to the Key Vault and what the managed identity's role scope actually is, and I'd test the new authentication path in a non-production environment before I'd let it anywhere near the pipeline that feeds the nightly refresh.
commonMistakes: Adding Key Vault but never actually rotating or revoking the originally exposed password
Granting the managed identity an overly broad role instead of least privilege
Overlooking that Self-Hosted Integration Runtime scenarios need separate credential handling
Not auditing who has Key Vault access after the migration
Leaving old plaintext parameter values sitting in publish history or ARM templates
Skipping validation of the new authentication path in a non-production environment first
keyPoints: Managed identity eliminates stored secrets for AAD-integrated targets
Key Vault-backed linked service for cases where a literal secret is unavoidable
Rotating/revoking the exposed credential is the actual fix for the departed contractor, not just hiding it
RBAC on Key Vault and the managed identity's role scope become the new access boundary to audit
Testing and validating the new authentication path before production rollout
Principle of least privilege when assigning the managed identity's role

Explicitly addresses rotating/revoking the already-exposed credential
Addresses least-privilege RBAC on the new identity/vault access

questions.title: dbt Mesh: Splitting a Monolithic Project Into Governed Domains
questions.prompt: Your dbt project has grown to 900+ models and six teams committing to the same repo, and PR review queues are now the bottleneck for every team, not just the ones making risky changes. Explain what dbt Mesh (multi-project architecture) actually changes at the mechanical level — cross-project ref(), public vs. private model access, model groups, and model contracts — and why splitting the project is a governance change, not just a repo reorganization.
questions.modelAnswer: dbt Mesh lets a model in one dbt project reference a model built by another dbt project via cross-project ref(), resolved through each project's published artifacts (manifest.json) rather than through a single shared DAG. Mechanically, a project that wants to expose a model to other projects marks it `access: public` inside a `group`; models left `private` (the default for grouped models, or ungrouped models by default access `protected`) cannot be ref()'d from outside their project or group. A model contract then pins the public model's column names and data types so the exposing team can change internals (SQL logic, materialization, intermediate steps) without breaking consumers, as long as the enforced interface doesn't change — and dbt refuses to run the model if the contract doesn't match the actual output. This is the real governance shift: splitting the repo alone just relocates merge conflicts, but public models + contracts convert 'please don't break my downstream model' from a tribal-knowledge request into something dbt enforces at build time, which is what actually lets each team own, version, and deploy their own project independently instead of queuing behind one shared PR review process.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the team the repo split is the easy 10% and the governance split is the real project. Before touching the repo, we need to agree on domain boundaries — which models genuinely belong to which team — and which of each team's models are actually meant to be consumed by others versus internal implementation detail. Those become the public, contracted models; everything else stays private and the owning team is free to refactor it without a cross-team conversation. I'd pilot this with one well-bounded domain first, get a contract break caught by CI instead of in production, and use that as the proof point before asking five more teams to adopt it. The thing I'd be explicit about with leadership is that this doesn't eliminate cross-team coordination — it just moves it from 'reviewing every PR' to 'reviewing contract changes on public models,' which is a much smaller and more defensible review surface.
commonMistakes: Treats dbt Mesh as purely a repo-splitting exercise with no governance component
Doesn't distinguish public/protected/private model access levels
Misses that contracts pin the interface (names/types), not the SQL logic, so internals can still evolve freely
Assumes cross-project ref() shares one DAG instead of resolving through published project artifacts
Underestimates the organizational work of agreeing on domain boundaries before the technical split
keyPoints: Explains cross-project ref() resolving through published artifacts, not a single shared DAG
Describes public/protected/private model access and groups
Explains model contracts as an enforced interface (names/types), decoupled from internal SQL
Frames the split as a governance change enabling independent team deploys, not just a repo reorg

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains cross-project ref() and public/private/protected access
Correctly explains model contracts as an enforced interface
Articulates the governance/organizational shift, not just the mechanics
Realistic rollout framing (pilot domain, independent deploys)

questions.title: dbt Semantic Layer at Scale: One Metric, Many Consumers
questions.prompt: A VP asks why 'active customers' returns three different numbers depending on whether someone pulls it from the executive Power BI dashboard, a Python notebook, or an ad hoc Snowflake query. Explain how dbt's Semantic Layer (MetricFlow, semantic models, and metrics defined in dbt) is meant to solve this at scale, and what has to be true organizationally — not just technically — for it to actually eliminate that drift.
questions.modelAnswer: MetricFlow lets you define a metric's logic — the measure, the dimensions it can be sliced by, any filters, and the join path back to its semantic model — exactly once, in dbt, as code. Every consumer (Power BI, a BI tool with a semantic layer integration, a notebook querying the Semantic Layer API, or an ad hoc query against the same underlying mart) then asks for 'active_customers by region' and gets SQL generated from that single definition, instead of each tool's author re-deriving the business logic ('active' = ordered in last 90 days? logged in last 30?) independently. Technically this closes the gap, but it only works organizationally if every consumer actually goes through the Semantic Layer instead of querying the underlying mart tables directly — if even one dashboard author bypasses it and writes their own SUM(), the drift comes right back. That means the Semantic Layer has to be positioned (and enforced via access patterns — e.g., restricting direct mart access, routing BI tools through the Semantic Layer API) as the only sanctioned path to that number, and the business has to agree on one definition of 'active' before it gets encoded, which is a negotiation problem, not a dbt problem.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by telling the VP the three numbers aren't a bug, they're three different unreviewed opinions about what 'active' means, and the Semantic Layer doesn't fix that by itself — it fixes it once we force all three teams to agree on one definition and then make it mechanically impossible to bypass. The MetricFlow piece is the easy part: define the metric once, point every BI tool and notebook at the Semantic Layer API instead of the raw tables. The harder part is the rollout — I'd get executive sponsorship to actually deprecate direct table access for that metric, otherwise someone's old dashboard keeps querying the mart directly and we're back to three numbers in six months. I'd frame it to leadership as: the technology is proven, the project risk is entirely in getting every team to give up their local definition.
commonMistakes: Describes the Semantic Layer purely as a caching or performance feature
Assumes defining the metric once in dbt automatically prevents drift without also restricting direct table access
Skips the organizational negotiation of agreeing on one business definition before encoding it
Doesn't mention that multiple consumer types (BI tools, notebooks, ad hoc SQL) all need to route through the same layer
keyPoints: Explains MetricFlow / semantic models defining measures, dimensions, and joins once
Notes multiple consumer types can query the same metric definition via the Semantic Layer API
Identifies that technical correctness alone doesn't stop drift if direct table access remains open
Frames the agreement on 'what active means' as an organizational negotiation, not a technical step

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains how MetricFlow/semantic models centralize metric logic
Identifies multiple consumer paths needing to route through the same layer
Explains the organizational precondition (agreement + enforcement) for it to work
Clear, VP-appropriate communication framing

questions.title: Snowflake Cost Governance: Resource Monitors and Multi-Warehouse Strategy
questions.prompt: Finance just flagged that the Snowflake bill tripled in a quarter with no corresponding growth in data volume or users. As the analytics engineering lead, explain the two main cost-governance levers available in Snowflake — resource monitors and warehouse sizing/isolation strategy — and why 'just add a resource monitor' is necessary but not sufficient to actually bring the bill under control.
questions.modelAnswer: Resource monitors set a credit quota (monthly, daily, or custom interval) against one or more warehouses and trigger actions — notify, suspend the warehouse, or suspend and cancel running queries — at defined thresholds, so they're a hard stop against runaway spend, not a way to reduce baseline spend. The deeper lever is warehouse strategy: Snowflake bills by warehouse-second while a warehouse is running, so cost is really a function of (a) how many warehouses are running, (b) how large each is, and (c) how long each stays up before auto-suspend kicks in. A common root cause behind a cost spike with flat data volume is workload bleed — ELT loads, BI dashboard queries, and ad hoc analyst queries all sharing one oversized always-on warehouse, so a single analyst's exploratory query or a dashboard with a short auto-suspend timeout keeps a large warehouse warm 24/7. The fix is isolating workloads onto separately sized warehouses (a small warehouse for ELT with tight auto-suspend, a dedicated warehouse for BI query concurrency, a separate one for ad hoc/analyst use with its own resource monitor) so each workload's cost is visible and controllable independently, rather than diagnosing one shared bill. Resource monitors then become the safety net on top of that isolated structure, not a substitute for it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell finance that a resource monitor alone is like putting a spending cap on a credit card without knowing which of five people is swiping it — it stops the bleeding but doesn't tell you why it happened. First move is pulling WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY to see which warehouse(s) actually drove the increase, because '3x spend, flat data volume' almost always means a workload or query pattern change, not a data growth problem. Then I look at auto-suspend settings and warehouse sharing — I'd bet money we'll find a BI warehouse with a long auto-suspend timeout that's also absorbing ad hoc analyst queries, keeping it warm way longer than the actual dashboard refresh cadence needs. My recommendation to leadership is always two-part: resource monitors as the guardrail everyone agrees to, and workload isolation as the actual fix, because a guardrail with no isolation just moves the pain to 'who gets cut off when we hit the cap.'
commonMistakes: Treats resource monitors as a cost-reduction tool rather than a spend-cap safety net
Doesn't connect warehouse-second billing to auto-suspend settings and workload sharing
Jumps straight to 'add a monitor' without first diagnosing which warehouse/workload drove the spike
Ignores that mixing ELT, BI, and ad hoc workloads on one warehouse is a common root cause
keyPoints: Explains resource monitors as threshold-based notify/suspend actions against a credit quota
Explains warehouse-second billing and the role of warehouse size + auto-suspend
Identifies workload isolation (ELT vs. BI vs. ad hoc) as the structural fix
Positions resource monitors as a safety net layered on top of isolation, not a substitute for it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains resource monitor mechanics (quota, thresholds, actions)
Correctly explains warehouse-second billing and auto-suspend's role in cost
Identifies workload isolation as the structural cost-governance lever
Clear diagnostic-first framing for a non-technical finance audience

questions.title: When Clustering Keys Help and When They Just Add Cost
questions.prompt: A teammate wants to add a clustering key to every large fact table in the warehouse 'to make queries faster.' Explain how Snowflake clustering actually works (micro-partitions, cluster depth, automatic reclustering), under what query patterns it genuinely helps, and when adding one is closer to pure cost with no real benefit.
questions.modelAnswer: Snowflake automatically divides table data into micro-partitions (roughly 50-500MB of uncompressed data each) as it's loaded, and stores metadata about the min/max values of each column within every micro-partition, which lets the query optimizer prune partitions that can't possibly match a filter — this is why Snowflake performs reasonably well on filtered queries even without any tuning. A clustering key tells Snowflake to try to co-locate rows with similar values of that key within the same micro-partitions, which improves pruning further specifically for queries that filter or join on that key — but it only helps when (a) the table is large enough that pruning actually matters (small tables scan fast regardless), (b) the clustering key has meaningfully high cardinality relative to how the data naturally loads (a key that's already roughly sorted by load order, like an ascending order_date, often doesn't need explicit clustering), and (c) query patterns consistently filter on that specific key rather than a different column each time. The cost side: once defined, Snowflake runs automatic reclustering as a background service that consumes credits every time new data arrives and disturbs the clustering order, so a clustering key on a table with heavy, continuous inserts/updates and a key that gets scrambled by every load can quietly become one of the largest line items on the bill for a benefit that never shows up in query time, because the queries hitting that table don't actually filter on that column. Before adding one, I'd check SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION to see actual clustering depth and confirm the dominant query filter pattern, not just add it reflexively.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back gently and ask what query pattern we're actually trying to speed up, because 'faster queries' isn't specific enough to justify a cost that bills continuously in the background. My rule of thumb: clustering pays off on big, mostly-append tables where the dominant filter column isn't already the natural load order — think a fact table that's loaded by source-system batch but queried by business date. It usually doesn't pay off on tables that are already naturally sorted by the filter column, or where query patterns are scattered across many different filter columns with no dominant one. Before recommending it anywhere, I'd pull SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION and the query history for that table first, show the actual depth number and the actual filter pattern, and let the data decide instead of applying it everywhere as a reflex — because I've seen teams add clustering keys to every big table and then get surprised months later that reclustering is a top-five cost line with nothing to show for it.
commonMistakes: Recommends clustering reflexively without checking whether the table's natural load order already approximates the key
Doesn't mention that automatic reclustering itself consumes credits on an ongoing basis
Confuses micro-partition pruning (automatic, free) with clustering keys (opt-in, has a maintenance cost)
Doesn't check SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION or actual query filter patterns before recommending a key
keyPoints: Explains automatic micro-partitioning and min/max pruning as the baseline, free mechanism
Explains what a clustering key changes (row co-location) and why it targets specific filter/join patterns
Identifies the automatic reclustering cost on tables with heavy continuous writes
Recommends checking actual clustering depth and query patterns before adding a key

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains micro-partitioning and pruning as the baseline mechanism
Correctly explains what a clustering key changes and when it helps
Identifies the ongoing reclustering cost and when it outweighs the benefit
Recommends evidence-based verification before adding a key

questions.title: Materialized Views in Snowflake: What You Trade for the Speed
questions.prompt: Explain what a materialized view in Snowflake actually is (versus a regular view and versus a dbt table materialization), how Snowflake keeps it up to date, and the cost/maintenance tradeoffs that make it the wrong choice for most dbt-managed transformation logic even though it looks like a shortcut to faster queries.
questions.modelAnswer: A regular view stores only its SQL definition and re-executes the full query every time it's referenced, so its 'freshness' is perfect by construction but its performance is identical to running the underlying query cold every time. A Snowflake materialized view instead persists the computed result and Snowflake's background service automatically and incrementally refreshes it whenever the underlying base table(s) change, so reads are fast (comparable to querying a table) and the data is kept current without any explicit refresh schedule or orchestration. That automatic maintenance is also the catch: Snowflake charges background compute credits continuously to keep a materialized view in sync, proportional to how frequently and how much the base table changes, and materialized views have real restrictions (one base table only, no joins, limited aggregate and window function support) that make them a poor fit for most multi-table dbt transformation logic. A dbt table materialization, by contrast, is a regular table rebuilt on an explicit schedule you control (via dbt runs, often incremental), so you pay compute only when you choose to run it, and you can freely join and transform across many sources — the tradeoff is that the data is only as fresh as the last run, not continuously live. In practice, materialized views fit a narrow case — a single-table rollup queried very frequently relative to how often the base table changes, where sub-second freshness genuinely matters and the base table isn't changing so often that the maintenance cost exceeds the savings. For most dbt mart-layer logic involving joins across staging models, a scheduled incremental table is both cheaper and more flexible.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it as: a materialized view trades 'you control when it costs money' for 'it's always fresh, and you pay for that continuously in the background.' It's genuinely useful for one specific shape of problem — a single-table aggregation that's hit constantly by dashboards and needs to be live, like a rolling count that updates every few minutes. It's a bad fit for the kind of multi-table, join-heavy marts dbt usually builds, both because of the single-base-table restriction and because you lose the ability to control and batch the compute cost the way an incremental dbt run lets you. If someone on the team proposes a materialized view as a performance fix, my first question is whether the real problem is query performance or data freshness — because if it's freshness, the materialized view's hidden background cost might cost more than just running the dbt job more often.
commonMistakes: Confuses materialized views with dbt's table materialization (they're not the same mechanism)
Doesn't mention the continuous background compute cost of automatic incremental refresh
Misses the join/base-table restrictions that make materialized views a poor fit for typical mart-layer dbt logic
Presents materialized views as a strictly better/faster alternative with no tradeoff
keyPoints: Contrasts regular view (re-executes), materialized view (persisted + auto-refreshed), and dbt table (explicitly scheduled rebuild)
Explains the continuous background refresh cost tied to base table change frequency
Notes materialized view restrictions (single base table, limited joins/aggregates)
Identifies the narrow use case where a materialized view is actually the right choice

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes view, materialized view, and dbt table materialization
Explains the automatic refresh mechanism and its ongoing cost
Identifies restrictions that make it unsuitable for most multi-table dbt logic
Gives a clear, correct use case where it is the right tool

questions.title: Airflow Deferrable Operators: Not Blocking a Worker Slot While Waiting
questions.prompt: A pipeline has a dozen sensor tasks each polling for a file to land, and they're consuming enough worker slots that other, unrelated DAGs are getting delayed. Explain what Airflow's deferrable operators (and the triggerer component) change about how that waiting is handled, and why this is a scaling concern specifically, not a correctness one.
questions.modelAnswer: A traditional sensor in poke mode occupies a worker slot for its entire wait, periodically waking up to check a condition and going back to sleep but never releasing the slot, so twelve long-polling sensors can tie up twelve worker slots for hours even though almost none of that time is spent doing real work. A deferrable operator (built on Airflow's triggerer component) instead suspends itself entirely after an initial check: it hands its wait condition off to a lightweight async trigger running in a separate triggerer process, releases its worker slot completely, and only resumes on a worker when the trigger actually fires (the condition is met or it times out). The triggerer can run many thousands of these async waits concurrently in a single process because they're not blocking threads, just awaited coroutines, so the actual compute and worker-slot cost of 'waiting for a file' drops from 'one slot per sensor for the whole wait' to 'near zero, until the moment work is ready to resume.' This is a scaling and cost concern, not a correctness one — a poke-mode sensor and its deferrable equivalent both correctly detect the condition and both eventually succeed or time out; the difference is entirely in how much of your worker capacity (and therefore how many unrelated DAGs can run concurrently) gets consumed while nothing is actually happening.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it with an analogy: a regular sensor is like twelve people standing in line holding a parking spot each, even though they're just waiting for a text message — a deferrable sensor is twelve people who leave and get a text when it's time to come back, freeing the spot in the meantime. The fix here isn't a correctness fix, nobody's pipeline is wrong — it's that we're burning worker capacity on waiting instead of working, which is exactly what's delaying the unrelated DAGs. I'd convert the file sensors to their deferrable equivalents (or a deferrable custom trigger if there isn't a built-in one for this exact file source), make sure the triggerer component is actually running and sized for the number of concurrent defers we'll have, and then show the before/after on worker slot utilization so it's clear this was a capacity problem, not a bug.
commonMistakes: Treats this as a bug in the sensors rather than a worker-slot capacity/scaling issue
Doesn't explain that the triggerer runs waits as async coroutines rather than blocking worker processes
Assumes deferrable operators change correctness or detection logic rather than just resource consumption during the wait
Forgets that the triggerer component itself needs to be running and appropriately sized
keyPoints: Explains poke-mode sensors occupying a full worker slot for the entire wait
Explains deferrable operators suspending to the triggerer and releasing the worker slot
Notes the triggerer runs many async waits concurrently in one process
Frames this correctly as a scaling/capacity issue, not a correctness issue

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains poke-mode sensor worker-slot consumption
Correctly explains deferrable operators and the triggerer mechanism
Correctly frames this as scaling/cost, not correctness
Clear practical remediation (convert sensors, size the triggerer)

questions.title: Dynamic DAG Generation: Power and Its Scheduler Cost
questions.prompt: A platform team wants to generate one Airflow DAG per client (currently 40 clients, growing) from a single Python template rather than hand-writing 40 near-identical DAG files. Explain how dynamic DAG generation actually works in Airflow, and the real operational cost it introduces at the scheduler level that a hand-written-DAG approach doesn't have.
questions.modelAnswer: Dynamic DAG generation means a single Python file (or a small set of files) programmatically constructs multiple DAG objects at parse time — typically by looping over a config source (a list in code, a database table, variables, or a config file) and calling a DAG-building function once per item, registering each resulting DAG object in the module's global namespace so Airflow's DAG file processor picks each one up as a distinct DAG. This is genuinely powerful for the 40-clients case: adding client 41 becomes a config change instead of a new file and a PR. The real cost is that Airflow's scheduler re-parses every DAG file on a recurring interval (min_file_process_interval) to detect new DAGs or changes, and if the config source for a dynamically generated set is slow to read (e.g., a live database query run at parse time rather than a cached/local file) or if the generation logic itself is computationally heavy, that parse cost is paid repeatedly, on every scheduler loop, for every one of those 40+ generated DAGs — which can measurably slow down the entire scheduler, not just the DAGs in question, because DAG parsing is a shared bottleneck resource. The standard mitigation is keeping the config source for generation fast and local (a cached file, not a live query) and keeping generation logic itself lightweight, since it runs on every parse, not once.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the team: yes, do it, but the thing that will bite us later isn't the DAG logic, it's where the 40 configs come from at parse time. If that's a live call to a database or an external API inside the DAG file, we've just made the scheduler's parsing loop dependent on that system's latency, multiplied by every parse interval, for every client — and that's the kind of thing that silently degrades the whole scheduler's health months after it ships, not something that fails loudly on day one. My recommendation is always: read the config from something fast and local, keep it out of the hot parse path, and I'd want to see DAG parse duration monitored from day one so if it creeps up as client count grows, we see it before it becomes 'the scheduler is slow and nobody knows why.'
commonMistakes: Describes dynamic DAG generation only at the code level without mentioning the scheduler's repeated re-parsing cost
Doesn't flag that a slow or live config source at parse time is the real risk, not the generation logic itself
Assumes this scales for free just because it reduces file count
Doesn't mention monitoring DAG parse duration as the way to catch this before it becomes a scheduler-wide problem
keyPoints: Explains looping over config to build multiple DAG objects registered in module globals
Explains that the scheduler re-parses DAG files on a recurring interval, not once
Identifies a slow/live config source at parse time as the main operational risk at scale
Recommends keeping generation logic and config source fast and local, with parse duration monitored

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the mechanics of generating multiple DAGs from one file
Correctly explains the scheduler's repeated DAG-parsing cost
Identifies the config-source latency risk specifically
Gives a concrete mitigation (fast local config, parse duration monitoring)

questions.title: Cross-DAG Dependencies: ExternalTaskSensor vs. Dataset-Driven Scheduling
questions.prompt: Team A's DAG must only start after Team B's upstream DAG finishes loading a table, but the two DAGs live in different repos owned by different teams. Explain the two main ways Airflow supports this cross-DAG dependency — ExternalTaskSensor and Datasets (asset-based scheduling) — and the tradeoff that should drive the choice between them.
questions.modelAnswer: ExternalTaskSensor works by having the downstream DAG poll the Airflow metadata database for the state of a specific task instance in a specific upstream DAG, matched by execution date/logical date (with an optional execution_delta or execution_date_fn if the schedules don't align exactly) — it's explicit and easy to reason about, but it tightly couples the two DAGs: the downstream DAG has to know the exact dag_id, task_id, and schedule alignment of the upstream one, and if the upstream team renames their DAG or changes its schedule, the downstream sensor silently breaks or misfires. Datasets (asset-aware scheduling) instead let the upstream task declare that it produces a given dataset (identified by a URI), and the downstream DAG is scheduled to trigger automatically whenever that dataset is updated, with no polling and no knowledge of the upstream DAG's internal structure, name, or schedule — it only needs to know the dataset identifier being produced, which decouples the two teams' DAGs from each other's implementation. The tradeoff: ExternalTaskSensor gives tighter, more explicit control (useful when you need to depend on a specific task's success, not just 'some update happened to this data') at the cost of coupling and polling overhead, while dataset-driven scheduling is the better default for cross-team dependencies specifically because it decouples ownership — Team B can rename or restructure their DAG freely as long as they keep declaring the same dataset output, and Team A's trigger just works.
questions.professionalAnswer: Between two different teams, I'd push toward Datasets almost every time, because the real problem with ExternalTaskSensor across team boundaries isn't technical, it's organizational — it means Team A's DAG has silent, undocumented knowledge of Team B's internal dag_id and schedule, and nobody finds out it broke until Team A's pipeline doesn't run. Datasets let each team keep ownership of their own DAG's internals; Team A just subscribes to 'this table was updated' and doesn't care how or when Team B's DAG produced it. I'd reserve ExternalTaskSensor for cases inside a single team's own DAGs where I genuinely need to know a specific task succeeded, not just that data showed up — that's a much narrower, intentional use than the default cross-team pattern.
commonMistakes: Doesn't mention the coupling risk of ExternalTaskSensor across team/ownership boundaries
Confuses dataset-driven scheduling with simple time-based scheduling
Doesn't explain execution_delta/schedule-alignment issues with ExternalTaskSensor
Recommends one mechanism universally without acknowledging the tradeoff context (within-team vs. cross-team)
keyPoints: Explains ExternalTaskSensor's polling-based dependency on a specific upstream dag_id/task_id/execution date
Explains Dataset-based scheduling triggering on declared data updates, decoupled from upstream internals
Identifies coupling vs. decoupling as the core tradeoff, especially across team ownership boundaries
Gives a sensible recommendation for cross-team dependencies specifically

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains ExternalTaskSensor mechanics and coupling risk
Correctly explains Dataset/asset-based scheduling mechanics
Articulates the coupling tradeoff clearly
Gives a sound recommendation for the cross-team scenario

questions.title: dbt Model Contracts and Versioning: Breaking Changes Without Breaking Everyone
questions.prompt: A team wants to change a widely-consumed dbt model's grain from one row per order to one row per order line, which changes its columns entirely. Explain how dbt model contracts and model versioning are meant to let that change happen safely across many downstream consumers, instead of everyone finding out when their query breaks.
questions.modelAnswer: A model contract declares and enforces the expected column names, data types, and (optionally) constraints for a model's output in its YAML config; once a contract is enforced, dbt will fail the model's build if the actual compiled SQL would produce a different shape than declared, which converts 'did I accidentally change this model's interface' from something discovered downstream into a build-time check. For a genuinely breaking change like a grain change, contracts alone aren't enough — that's exactly what model versioning exists for: you define a new version of the model (e.g., orders.v2) with its own contract reflecting the new grain and columns, while the original version continues to exist and serve existing consumers unchanged. Consumers then migrate to the new version on their own schedule by updating their ref() to point at the specific version they want, and once you're confident all critical consumers have migrated, you deprecate and eventually remove the old version. This turns a breaking change from a flag day where everything has to move at once into a managed migration with a visible list of who's still on the old version, which is the only way to do this safely once a model has many downstream consumers you don't control.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the team: don't change the existing model in place, ship it as a new version. Add orders.v2 with the new grain and its own contract, leave orders.v1 (or unversioned orders) exactly as it is, and let every downstream owner move to v2 when they're ready rather than on our timeline. The contract on each version is what actually lets me sleep at night here, because if someone's SQL in a different project accidentally drifts in a way that would silently change the output shape, the build fails loudly instead of someone's exec dashboard quietly going wrong. Before I'd even propose this to the team, I'd pull every known downstream ref() I can find — exposures, cross-project refs if we're on dbt Mesh — so the migration has a real checklist instead of us finding out who broke three weeks later.
commonMistakes: Confuses model contracts (shape enforcement) with model versioning (parallel versions for breaking changes)
Proposes changing the existing model in place for a breaking grain change instead of versioning it
Doesn't mention tracking/identifying downstream consumers before making the change
Assumes a contract alone prevents breaking changes, rather than versioning being the actual mechanism for that
keyPoints: Explains model contracts enforcing column names/types at build time
Explains model versioning as parallel, independently-contracted versions for breaking changes

questions.title: Fix a Non-SARGable, Non-Covering Query Under Load
questions.prompt:
You're handed this production query that's doing a full clustered index scan on a 40-million-row table, confirmed via SET STATISTICS IO showing logical reads in the hundreds of thousands:

SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, OrderDate, TotalDue
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader
WHERE CONVERT(VARCHAR(10), OrderDate, 101) = '06/15/2013'
   AND UPPER(Status) = 'SHIPPED';

Rewrite the query to be SARGable, and write the covering index you'd create to support it, explaining your column order choice.
questions.modelAnswer: There are two non-SARGable predicates here, and both need fixing. CONVERT(VARCHAR(10), OrderDate, 101) wraps the date column in a function, forcing a scan even if an index exists; UPPER(Status) does the same to the status column. The date predicate should be rewritten as a half-open range against the raw column; the status predicate should compare against the literal in its natural case, relying on the column's collation to be case-insensitive rather than forcing a transformation on every row. For the covering index, the equality predicate (Status) should lead the key, since equality columns belong before range columns in a composite index — this lets SQL Server seek to the exact Status value, then scan only the OrderDate range within that narrower slice — and the remaining selected columns go into INCLUDE so the plan never needs a Key Lookup back to the clustered index.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point out there are actually two separate problems stacked in that one WHERE clause, not one. The CONVERT around OrderDate and the UPPER around Status are both doing the same damage — wrapping the column so the index can't be used no matter how well it's built. I'd rewrite the date as a range against the raw column and drop the UPPER, trusting the collation to handle case. Then for the index, I always put the equality column first — Status — because that lets SQL Server narrow down to an exact value before it even has to think about the date range, and I'd include the rest of the selected columns so we get a fully covering seek with no extra trip back to the clustered index.
questions.example:
-- SARGable rewrite
SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, OrderDate, TotalDue
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader
WHERE Status = 'Shipped'
  AND OrderDate >= '2013-06-15' AND OrderDate < '2013-06-16';

-- Covering index: equality column first, then the range column, then INCLUDE the rest
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_SalesOrderHeader_Status_OrderDate
ON Sales.SalesOrderHeader (Status, OrderDate)
INCLUDE (OrderID, CustomerID, TotalDue);
commonMistakes: Only fixes one of the two non-SARGable predicates
Puts the range column before the equality column in the index key
Forgets INCLUDE columns, leaving a Key Lookup in the plan
Assumes UPPER() is needed without checking the column's collation
keyPoints: Identifies both non-SARGable predicates
Rewrites the date predicate as a range
Removes the function wrapper on Status, citing collation
Designs index key order correctly: equality before range
Makes the index covering with INCLUDE

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly rewrites both non-SARGable predicates
Index design uses correct key order (equality before range)
Index is fully covering via INCLUDE
Explains reasoning, not just the syntax
