questions.title: A New Clustering Key Didn't Move the Needle
questions.prompt: You added a clustering key to a large Snowflake table two weeks ago expecting a specific slow query to speed up, but query time hasn't changed and the reclustering credit cost is now a visible line item. Walk through how you'd diagnose why the clustering key isn't helping.
questions.modelAnswer: First I'd check SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION for the table to see whether the table has actually reached a good clustering state — if average_depth is still high two weeks later, the table may still be mid-reclustering (very large tables can take a while), or the column chosen simply doesn't have enough cardinality/selectivity for clustering to meaningfully separate micro-partitions by its values. If clustering depth has actually improved, the next check is whether the slow query is really filtering or joining on the clustered column at all — a surprisingly common mistake is clustering on the column someone assumed was the dominant filter, when the actual EXPLAIN/query profile shows the real bottleneck is a different predicate, a join explosion, or a lack of pruning on a completely different column. I'd pull the query profile for the actual slow query and check partitions scanned versus partitions total; if that ratio didn't improve even though clustering depth did, the clustering key isn't actually on the critical path for this query, and continuing to pay reclustering cost for it has no justification. At that point the fix is either re-clustering on the column that actually matches the real filter pattern, or dropping the clustering key altogether if the query's real bottleneck isn't partition pruning at all (e.g., it's a lack of a different index-like structure, a bad join order, or genuinely needs a bigger/different warehouse).
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start exactly where I should have started before adding the key: what does the query profile actually show as the bottleneck? If I didn't check that up front, this is the moment to go back and check SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION and the real query's partition-scanned ratio, because one of two things is true — either the table genuinely isn't clustered well yet, or it is, and the clustering key was never on the critical path for this specific query in the first place. I'd be honest with the team if it's the second case: we're paying ongoing reclustering cost for a key that isn't helping this query, and the right move is either re-clustering on the actual bottleneck column or dropping it, not leaving it in place out of sunk-cost reluctance.
commonMistakes: Assumes the clustering key must be working just because it was added, without checking SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION
Doesn't verify the slow query actually filters/joins on the clustered column via its query profile
Doesn't consider that the real bottleneck might be unrelated to partition pruning entirely (join order, warehouse sizing)
Keeps paying ongoing reclustering cost for a key that isn't improving the target query, out of reluctance to undo the change
keyPoints: Checks SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION to confirm actual clustering state/depth
Verifies the slow query's real filter/join pattern via its query profile, not assumption
Checks partitions-scanned ratio to confirm whether pruning actually improved for that query
Is willing to re-cluster on a different column or drop the key if it isn't on the critical path

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly uses SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION to verify clustering state
Verifies the actual query's filter/join pattern against the clustered column
Checks partition-pruning improvement specifically, not just depth
Willing to reverse the decision if evidence doesn't support it

questions.title: Cross-DAG Dependency Silently Stops Triggering
questions.prompt: A downstream DAG that depends on an upstream DAG via ExternalTaskSensor has been quietly not running for the past week — no errors, no alerts, it's just sitting there. Walk through how you'd diagnose why.
questions.modelAnswer: A silently-not-triggering ExternalTaskSensor almost always means the match condition it's polling for stopped being satisfied, not that anything crashed — so I'd first check whether the upstream DAG's schedule, dag_id, or the specific task_id being watched changed recently (a rename, a schedule interval change, or the task being restructured into a TaskGroup which changes its effective task_id). The sensor matches by execution/logical date using an execution_delta or execution_date_fn, so if the upstream DAG's schedule shifted even slightly, the sensor may now be looking for a logical date that the upstream DAG never actually runs with, causing it to poll forever until timeout without ever finding a match — which looks exactly like silent non-triggering rather than a loud error. I'd check the sensor's own task logs for what execution date it's actually searching for on each poke, compare that against the upstream DAG's actual run history, and confirm the dag_id/task_id strings still match exactly. If everything matches and it's still not triggering, I'd check whether the sensor itself is stuck queued behind a pool or concurrency limit rather than actually executing pokes at all. This is also the concrete case for recommending a move to Dataset-based scheduling instead, since it removes this entire class of silent breakage by not depending on execution-date alignment between two DAGs' schedules.
questions.professionalAnswer: Nine times out of ten with a silent ExternalTaskSensor failure, someone changed something about the upstream DAG — its schedule, its dag_id, or restructured the task the sensor is watching — and nobody updated the sensor's execution_delta or target IDs to match. I'd check the sensor's own logs for the exact logical date it's searching for versus the upstream DAG's actual run history, because a mismatch there explains 'polls forever, never errors, never triggers' perfectly. Once I fix the immediate issue, I'd use this incident to make the case for migrating this dependency to Datasets, because this exact failure mode — two DAGs silently drifting out of schedule alignment with each other — is specifically what asset-based scheduling removes.
commonMistakes: Assumes something crashed when a silent non-trigger is actually a logical-date mismatch that never satisfies the sensor's match condition
Doesn't check whether the upstream DAG's schedule, dag_id, or task_id changed recently
Doesn't check the sensor's own logs for the specific logical date it's searching for
Misses pool/concurrency limits as an alternative explanation for a stuck sensor task
keyPoints: Identifies a schedule/dag_id/task_id mismatch with the upstream DAG as the likely root cause
Checks the sensor's actual logical-date search target in its logs against upstream run history
Considers pool/concurrency limits as an alternative cause of a stuck sensor
Recommends Dataset-based scheduling as a structural fix to this class of failure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses a logical-date/ID mismatch as the likely cause
Describes a concrete verification method (sensor logs vs. upstream run history)
Considers an alternative cause (pool/concurrency limits)
Recommends a structural fix (Datasets) to prevent recurrence

questions.title: Two BI Tools Disagree on a Semantic Layer Metric
questions.prompt: Power BI and a data science notebook are both querying the same dbt Semantic Layer metric, net_revenue, for the same month and region, but they're returning different numbers. Walk through how you'd diagnose this, given that the metric is supposed to be defined exactly once.
questions.modelAnswer: If the metric is genuinely defined once and both tools are genuinely querying through the Semantic Layer, the most likely explanations are a caching/staleness mismatch (one consumer is reading a cached result from before the underlying models last ran, the other is hitting a fresh query) or a time-window/grain mismatch in how each tool is requesting the data (one requesting by order_date, the other by a different time dimension if the semantic model exposes more than one, or a timezone boundary difference causing 'October' to include slightly different rows). The first thing I'd actually verify, though, is whether both tools are really going through the Semantic Layer at all — it's common for an existing Power BI report built before the Semantic Layer existed to still query the underlying mart table directly rather than through the MetricFlow-generated SQL, in which case the two numbers were never guaranteed to match in the first place because only one of them is actually using the governed definition. I'd check each tool's actual generated SQL/query log, compare it against the Semantic Layer's generated SQL for the same request, and if the Power BI report turns out to be hitting the raw table, that's the root cause and the fix is migrating that specific report to query through the Semantic Layer connector rather than debugging the metric definition at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I touch the metric definition, I check whether both consumers are actually using it — that's the single most common reason 'one source of truth' numbers disagree: an old report built before the Semantic Layer existed, still pointed at the raw table. I'd pull the actual query/SQL each tool generated for this request and compare them side by side. If both are genuinely routed through the Semantic Layer and still disagree, then I'm looking at caching staleness or a subtle time-window/timezone difference in how each tool framed the request — but I wouldn't assume that until I've ruled out the much more common 'one of these isn't actually using the shared definition' explanation first.
commonMistakes: Assumes both tools are definitely using the Semantic Layer without verifying their actual generated query/SQL
Jumps to debugging the metric's YAML definition before confirming both consumers route through it
Doesn't consider caching/staleness as a cause when both genuinely do use the Semantic Layer
Doesn't consider timezone or time-window framing differences between the two requests
keyPoints: Verifies both consumers are actually routing through the Semantic Layer before anything else
Compares each tool's actual generated SQL/query for the request
Considers caching/staleness as a cause when both genuinely use the shared definition
Considers time-window/timezone framing differences between requests

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Verifies both consumers actually query through the Semantic Layer first
Proposes comparing actual generated SQL between the two tools
Considers caching/staleness as a secondary cause
Considers time-window/timezone framing as a secondary cause

questions.title: A Materialized View Stops Reflecting New Data
questions.prompt: A Snowflake materialized view that's always stayed current has started showing stale numbers — the underlying base table clearly has new rows, but the materialized view hasn't picked them up for several hours. Walk through your diagnosis.
questions.modelAnswer: A materialized view's background refresh can suspend itself or fall behind for a few distinct reasons, so I'd check each: first, whether the materialized view's automatic refresh has actually been suspended — this can happen if its warehouse (materialized views use a system-managed warehouse resource, separate from user warehouses, but it can still be resource-constrained) is unavailable, or if someone explicitly ran ALTER MATERIALIZED VIEW ... SUSPEND for maintenance and never resumed it. Second, I'd check whether the base table underwent a bulk operation the materialized view's incremental refresh can't handle efficiently — a very large bulk load or a schema change on the base table can cause the refresh to fall significantly behind or require a fuller recomputation, which shows up as a growing staleness window rather than an outright error. Third, I'd check Snowflake's materialized view refresh history (available via ACCOUNT_USAGE or SHOW MATERIALIZED VIEWS / describing the object) for actual error states on recent refresh attempts, since a refresh can fail silently from the consumer's point of view if nobody's watching that specific history. I would not assume this is a one-off and just manually force a refresh without finding the actual cause, because if it's a suspended state or a recurring failure, it will just happen again.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd check three things in order: is the materialized view actually suspended right now (ALTER MATERIALIZED VIEW ... RESUME is the fix if so, but I want to know why it was suspended first), did the base table have an unusual bulk operation recently that the incremental refresh choked on, and does the refresh history show actual failures rather than just being slow. I wouldn't just force a manual refresh and move on, because if the underlying cause is a suspended state from a maintenance window someone forgot to close out, or a recurring refresh failure, this exact staleness comes right back. I'd also use this incident to double check whether this materialized view was really the right tool for this table in the first place, since this is exactly the kind of hidden operational fragility that doesn't show up until something unusual happens to the base table.
commonMistakes: Force-refreshes the materialized view manually without identifying why it stopped auto-refreshing
Doesn't check whether the materialized view is in a suspended state
Doesn't consider a bulk load or schema change on the base table as a cause of refresh lag
Doesn't check actual refresh history/error states, assuming 'stale' means 'just slow'
keyPoints: Checks whether the materialized view's automatic refresh has been suspended
Considers a bulk load or schema change on the base table as a cause of refresh lag or failure
Checks actual refresh history for error states rather than assuming simple lag
Avoids a blind manual force-refresh without identifying the root cause

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Checks suspended-refresh state as a primary hypothesis
Considers base-table bulk load/schema change as a cause
Checks actual refresh history for failures
Avoids treating a manual force-refresh as a real fix without root cause

questions.title: Deferred Airflow Tasks Are Stuck Forever
questions.prompt: After converting several sensors to deferrable operators, you notice a growing number of tasks sitting in a 'deferred' state well past when their condition should have been satisfied, never resuming. Walk through how you'd diagnose this.
questions.modelAnswer: Tasks stuck in deferred state that never resume point directly at the triggerer component — a deferred task hands its wait off to an async trigger running inside the triggerer process, and if the triggerer isn't running at all, is undersized relative to the number of concurrent deferred triggers it needs to run, or has crashed/restarted and lost in-memory trigger state, tasks will sit deferred indefinitely with no worker-side error, because from the worker's perspective it correctly handed off the wait and is just waiting to be told to resume. I'd first check whether the triggerer process is actually running and healthy in this deployment (it's a separate component from the scheduler and workers, and it's easy for a team new to deferrable operators to not have deployed it at all, or to have deployed only one under-resourced instance). If it is running, I'd check its own logs for errors on the specific trigger classes involved, and check how many concurrent triggers it's managing against its configured capacity, since a single triggerer process handling far more concurrent async waits than expected can start silently falling behind or dropping triggers under memory pressure. I'd also confirm this started exactly when the sensors were converted, which would point squarely at either a missing/undersized triggerer or a bug in how the specific operator's trigger class was implemented, rather than anything else changing concurrently.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is almost always the triggerer, because that's the one new moving part we introduced by switching to deferrable operators. First question: is a triggerer process even running in this deployment, and if so, is it just one instance now expected to handle a lot more concurrent deferred tasks than it was sized for? I'd check its logs directly for errors on the specific trigger classes, and I'd check whether it's been restarted recently, since a triggerer restart can lose in-flight trigger state and leave tasks stuck. Given that this started right after the sensor conversion, I'm treating the triggerer as guilty until proven innocent before I look anywhere else.
commonMistakes: Investigates worker or scheduler logs first instead of recognizing this as a triggerer-specific symptom
Doesn't check whether a triggerer process is running and healthy at all
Doesn't consider triggerer capacity/sizing relative to the number of concurrent deferred tasks
Misses that the timing correlation with the sensor conversion is itself diagnostic
keyPoints: Identifies the triggerer component as the primary suspect for stuck deferred tasks
Checks whether the triggerer is running at all, and whether it's appropriately sized/resourced
Checks triggerer-specific logs for errors on the relevant trigger classes
Uses the timing correlation with the sensor conversion as a diagnostic clue

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the triggerer component as the root-cause area
Checks triggerer running state and sizing/capacity
Checks triggerer-specific logs for errors
Uses timing correlation with the recent change as a diagnostic signal

questions.title: Design review: capacity and workspace governance for 3,000 seats
questions.prompt: You're the Power BI architect presenting to a review board for a 3,000-seat enterprise tenant. Design the capacity, workspace, and governance model across dev/test/prod, including the Premium-vs-Fabric capacity sizing tradeoff, and explain specifically how you'd prevent one bad dataset refresh from starving the entire capacity for everyone else.
questions.modelAnswer: Workspace/environment structure: separate workspaces (and ideally separate capacities or at least separate capacity-assigned pools) for dev, test, and prod, so a developer's experimental semantic model never competes for the same compute as a production dashboard the CFO is watching live. Role discipline follows Lesson 69's four roles strictly: a small platform-governance group holds Admin everywhere; day-to-day builders get Contributor in dev/test and a tightly controlled Member/Contributor split in prod; end users consume only through apps, never direct workspace access. Capacity sizing: Fabric (F-SKU) capacities are the modern unit and, since Fabric now houses Power BI alongside data engineering and real-time analytics workloads on shared capacity, they make sense if the organization is likely to adopt other Fabric workloads — otherwise a Premium (P-SKU) capacity is functionally equivalent for pure Power BI use and may be the simpler choice to procure today. Size for peak concurrent refresh-plus-interactive-query load, not average load, since Premium/Fabric capacities enforce a shared compute pool across every workspace assigned to them — undersizing means every workspace on that capacity feels the pain of the busiest one. The core risk — one bad dataset refresh starving the whole capacity — is addressed on three levels: (1) workload management settings on the capacity, which let an admin cap how much of the capacity's resources a given workload (like Dataset refresh) can consume, preventing one workload type from monopolizing everything; (2) capacity-level autoscale (where available) to absorb genuine spikes rather than letting them degrade every other workspace; (3) governance controls on model design itself — refresh timeouts, dataset size limits, and a review gate before a new large or complex model goes onto a shared production capacity, so the 'bad refresh' is caught before deployment rather than mitigated after the fact. I'd also keep at least one workspace's worth of headroom unassigned/reserved so a true outlier incident has somewhere to be isolated rather than immediately re-triggering a capacity-wide incident.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd present this in three layers, because 'capacity planning' actually means three different decisions stacked on top of each other. First, environment separation: dev, test, and prod get their own workspaces, and ideally their own capacity assignment, so an experiment in dev literally cannot compete for compute with a live executive dashboard in prod — that's non-negotiable. Second, the capacity SKU decision: Fabric capacities are where Microsoft's putting their investment, and if we think we'll ever touch other Fabric workloads, I'd go Fabric now rather than migrate later; if we're purely a Power BI shop with no near-term Fabric ambitions, Premium is functionally the same thing today and might be the simpler procurement. Either way, I size for peak concurrent load, not average, because everyone on that capacity shares the same compute pool — undersizing doesn't just slow down the heavy workspace, it slows down everyone. Third, and this is the question I know the board actually cares about: how do we stop one bad refresh from taking everyone down. My answer is workload management settings at the capacity level — we can cap how much of the capacity a given workload type, like dataset refresh, is allowed to consume, so it physically can't eat the whole pool. On top of that, I'd put a review gate in front of any new large model going into production, and keep a sliver of reserved headroom so a genuine outlier incident has somewhere to land instead of immediately becoming everyone's problem.
commonMistakes: Sizing capacity for average load instead of peak concurrent load
Not separating dev/test/prod onto distinct workspace/capacity boundaries
Assuming Premium and Fabric are interchangeable without considering future Fabric workload adoption
Missing workload management settings as the actual control for preventing one workload from starving the capacity
No review gate before large/complex models go into a shared production capacity
keyPoints: Dev/test/prod separation at the workspace and ideally capacity level
Role discipline (Admin/Member/Contributor/Viewer) enforced consistently across environments
Fabric vs Premium is a strategic bet on future Fabric workload adoption, not a pure feature gap today
Capacity sizing must target peak concurrent load across the shared pool
Workload management settings cap per-workload resource consumption to prevent starvation
A pre-deployment review gate catches 'bad refresh' risk before it reaches shared capacity

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a coherent dev/test/prod workspace and role model
Correctly reasons through Premium vs Fabric capacity tradeoffs
Sizes capacity against peak shared-pool load, not average
Proposes a concrete mechanism (workload management) preventing one refresh from starving the capacity
Includes a governance/review-gate layer, not just technical settings

questions.title: Architecture Review: A Multi-Tenant Power BI Embedded Platform for 200 External Customers
questions.prompt: Your company is building a SaaS product that embeds Power BI reports for 200 external customers, with a hard requirement that one customer must never be able to see even a trace of another customer's data. Design the architecture: the app-owns-data model, capacity sizing, and specifically how you'd guarantee tenant isolation.
questions.modelAnswer: For an external-facing SaaS product, this is the app-owns-data embedding model, not user-owns-data: the application authenticates to the Power BI service using a dedicated service principal (or master user account, though service principal is the modern, recommended path), and every customer who opens the embedded report is really an anonymous end user as far as Power BI is concerned -- the application itself controls what they see, through the embed token the app generates for each session. Tenant isolation, the hard requirement here, has to be enforced at two layers, not one: first, row-level security on the semantic model, scoped per customer, so even if every customer's data lives in one shared semantic model (the efficient, common pattern at this scale), the RLS role filters every query to that customer's rows only, and the embed token generation call explicitly specifies which RLS role and identity to apply for that session -- getting this binding wrong, generating a token without the correct effective identity, is the single most dangerous failure mode in this architecture, because it would let a customer's session see unfiltered data. Second, I would not rely on RLS alone for a hard '200 customers, zero tolerance for crossover' requirement -- I'd add workspace-level separation for at least any customer whose contract or risk profile demands it, with the option of per-customer or per-tier workspaces rather than always sharing one semantic model, trading operational simplicity for a harder isolation boundary where the business actually needs one. Capacity sizing: at 200 external customers, this needs a Premium or Fabric (F-SKU) capacity rather than per-user licensing, since end customers don't hold Power BI licenses in the embedded model; sizing targets peak concurrent embedded sessions plus whatever refresh load the shared or per-tenant semantic models generate, and I'd load-test with simulated concurrent sessions before committing to a specific SKU rather than estimating from a seat count that doesn't actually apply here. I'd also insist on an audit trail specifically logging which RLS role/identity was applied to every embed token generated, so an isolation failure -- however unlikely -- would be immediately traceable rather than discovered by a customer complaint.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd be most careful to get right here isn't the capacity sizing, it's the embed token generation, because that's the one place a mistake actually leaks data between customers. This is the app-owns-data model -- our application, not the individual customer, authenticates to Power BI, and every customer session is really just an identity our app asserts when it generates that session's embed token. If every customer shares one semantic model for efficiency, which is the common pattern at this scale, the embed token has to carry the correct RLS role and customer identity every single time, with no exceptions and no fallback path that generates a token without it -- that's the one bug that would actually violate the hard requirement here. Given how much is riding on 'zero tolerance for crossover,' I wouldn't lean on RLS as the only control for every customer -- for higher-risk or larger customers I'd put them in their own workspace entirely, so there's a harder boundary than a filter that has to be applied correctly on every single token. On capacity, since these are external users with no Power BI licenses of their own, this has to run on a Premium or Fabric capacity sized for peak concurrent embedded sessions, and I wouldn't commit to a SKU without actually load-testing simulated concurrency first. And I'd want every embed token's RLS role and identity logged, so if anything ever did go wrong, we'd know immediately and exactly how, instead of finding out from a customer.
commonMistakes: Confuses app-owns-data embedding with user-owns-data licensing, assuming customers need Power BI accounts
Treats RLS alone as sufficient for a zero-tolerance isolation requirement without considering workspace-level separation for higher-risk tenants
Doesn't identify embed token generation (RLS role/identity binding) as the actual point of failure risk
Sizes capacity by a per-user seat count instead of peak concurrent embedded sessions
Doesn't propose auditing which RLS role/identity was applied per session
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the app-owns-data embedding model and service principal authentication
Identifies embed token generation (RLS role/identity binding) as the critical isolation control and failure risk
Proposes workspace-level separation as a harder boundary for tenants where RLS alone is too risky
Sizes Premium/Fabric capacity against peak concurrent embedded sessions, not seat counts
Proposes auditing of RLS role/identity per embed token for traceability

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs the app-owns-data embedding architecture
Identifies embed token/RLS binding as the critical tenant-isolation control
Proposes workspace-level separation as an additional isolation layer where warranted
Sizes capacity correctly for an external embedded scenario
Proposes auditability of per-session RLS/identity binding

questions.title: Workspace Topology and Deployment Pipelines Across 40 Business Units
questions.prompt: Your company has grown to 40 business units, each of which created its own Power BI workspace years ago with no naming convention, inconsistent owners, and no promotion process — reports go straight from a developer's laptop to "production" with a Publish click. You're hired as the first BI platform lead and asked to redesign the tenant's workspace topology and release process without a multi-month reorganization that halts reporting. Describe the workspace structure you'd move teams toward, how deployment pipelines fit in, and how you'd sequence the migration.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd move from ad hoc workspaces to a structure organized by domain/business-unit with a consistent naming convention and a workspace role per environment: Dev, Test, and Prod workspaces per domain, wired together with Power BI deployment pipelines so content is promoted (not re-published) across stages with rule-based parameter swaps for data sources. Each domain gets a named content owner and a workspace admin distinct from individual report authors, with Member/Contributor/Viewer roles mapped to actual job functions rather than everyone being an admin. I'd separate a small number of shared, certified semantic-model workspaces from report-only workspaces, so datasets are built once and reused rather than duplicated per business unit. For sequencing, I wouldn't do a big-bang migration: I'd pick one cooperative, high-visibility domain as a pilot, stand up its Dev/Test/Prod pipeline, prove the promotion workflow and rollback path, then use it as the reference pattern to onboard other domains in waves, prioritizing the ones with the worst governance debt (unowned workspaces, broken refreshes) first. Old workspaces get frozen for new publishing but left readable until migration completes, avoiding a hard cutover that breaks live dashboards mid-transition.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by asking what's actually breaking today versus what's just untidy — a naming mess is annoying, but reports going live without any test step is the thing causing incidents, so that's what I'd fix first. My instinct is a domain-based workspace model: one Dev/Test/Prod trio per business unit, connected through deployment pipelines so 'promote' replaces 'republish.' I'd pull shared semantic models into their own workspaces, separate from the report workspaces, so I'm not fighting dataset duplication at the same time as fixing process. On rollout, I'd never try to migrate 40 business units at once — I'd find one or two cooperative teams, get the Dev/Test/Prod pipeline running end to end, including how we handle data-source parameters and rollback, and use that as a proof point. Then I'd go after the domains causing the most pain first, not alphabetically, because that's where I earn trust fastest. The old workspaces I'd freeze rather than delete, so nothing breaks for end users while the migration is in flight. I'd also be upfront with leadership that this is a quarters-long change, not a weekend project, and set checkpoints so progress is visible along the way.
commonMistakes: Attempting a single big-bang migration of all 40 business units at once
Giving every report author workspace admin rights instead of scoping roles to actual responsibilities
Treating deployment pipelines as optional polish rather than the core promotion mechanism
Letting each business unit keep its own copy of the same semantic model instead of consolidating to shared, certified datasets
Deleting old workspaces immediately instead of freezing them during a phased cutover
Designing the ideal end-state without a realistic, risk-ranked sequencing plan
keyPoints: Domain/business-unit workspace structure with Dev/Test/Prod environments per domain
Deployment pipelines used for promotion with parameter rules per stage, not manual republishing
Separation of shared semantic-model workspaces from report-only workspaces
Role assignment mapped to real responsibilities, not blanket admin access
Phased, risk-prioritized migration sequencing with a pilot domain
A transition plan that avoids breaking live reports during cutover

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Workspace topology design is coherent and scalable across many business units
Correct use of deployment pipelines as the promotion mechanism
Realistic, risk-aware migration sequencing
Addresses governance roles and shared semantic-model reuse

questions.title: Dynamic RLS for a Multi-Tenant Reseller Model at Scale
questions.prompt: A single large semantic model serves 300 reseller accounts, each of which should see only their own transactions, and some resellers have sub-accounts that should see a further-restricted slice. The model already has complex relationships and several bidirectional filters for other reporting needs, and the business wants new resellers onboarded by adding a row to a table, not a Power BI redeploy. Design the row-level security approach, and address the design tradeoffs and testing risks specific to a model this complex.
questions.modelAnswer: This calls for dynamic RLS, not static per-reseller roles: a security mapping table joined to the fact or dimension table, filtered using USERPRINCIPALNAME() so a single role definition covers all 300 resellers, and onboarding becomes a row insert into the mapping table rather than a model change. For sub-accounts with a further-restricted slice, I'd model the mapping table with a hierarchy (reseller id, sub-account id) and apply the filter at the lowest grain needed, rather than stacking multiple roles, which Power BI combines with OR logic and can accidentally widen access instead of narrowing it. Given the model already has bidirectional filters, I'd audit where RLS filters propagate through those relationships, because ambiguous or bidirectional paths are exactly where RLS silently fails to restrict data or forces expensive cross-filtering on every visual. Where possible, I'd switch relationships touched by the RLS filter path to single-direction and use explicit measures for the few bidirectional use cases that need it. For testing, "View As" only impersonates roles as the tester's own identity for dynamic RLS, so I'd build a small set of test user accounts (or use the admin API) representing a sampling of resellers and sub-accounts, and validate both correctness and performance under those identities before rollout, not just functionally spot-check the filter.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by separating two problems that look the same but aren't: correctness of who-sees-what, and the design tradeoffs that come with enforcing that at 300 accounts. For correctness, a mapping table driven by USERPRINCIPALNAME() is the only approach that scales to 'onboard by adding a row' — static roles would mean a deployment every time a reseller signs up, which the business explicitly ruled out. For the sub-account wrinkle, I'd be careful that multiple roles in Power BI OR together rather than AND, so I'd model the hierarchy into the mapping table itself rather than relying on role-stacking to narrow access, because that's a classic way teams accidentally over-expose data. Then I'd go looking for where this bites the model — specifically any bidirectional relationships the RLS filter has to cross, since that's where a report that's fine for an admin can silently leak data or behave unpredictably for a filtered reseller. I'd want to walk the model's relationship diagram before writing a single DAX filter, not after. And on testing, I'd flag early that 'Test as role' doesn't actually prove security for dynamic RLS since it runs as the tester's own identity — so I'd insist on test accounts or the admin API to validate both the right people see the right rows and that the design holds up at a realistic grain.
questions.example: RLS filter on the mapping table: [UserMapping] = LOOKUPVALUE(ResellerAccess[AccountEmail], ResellerAccess[AccountEmail], USERPRINCIPALNAME())
commonMistakes: Using static per-reseller roles that require a model redeploy for every new account
Stacking multiple roles for sub-account restrictions without realizing roles combine with OR logic
Ignoring bidirectional relationships that the RLS filter path crosses, causing either leakage or unpredictable behavior
Relying solely on 'Test as role' to validate dynamic RLS, which tests as the tester's own identity rather than the target user
Not validating behavior under a filtered identity before rollout
Applying the RLS filter at too high a grain, forcing unnecessary cross-filtering for simple cases
keyPoints: Dynamic RLS via a mapping table and USERPRINCIPALNAME() to support row-based onboarding
Hierarchical mapping design to handle sub-account restriction without role-stacking pitfalls
Audit of bidirectional/ambiguous relationships along the RLS filter path
Preference for single-direction relationships where RLS filters propagate
Realistic testing strategy beyond 'Test as role' (test accounts, admin API)
Design-level validation under filtered identities, not just functional correctness

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct dynamic RLS design supporting row-based onboarding
Handles sub-account hierarchy without role-stacking errors
Identifies and addresses bidirectional-relationship design risk
Realistic testing strategy for dynamic RLS

questions.title: Breaking the Cycle of Duplicated Report-Local Semantic Models
questions.prompt: Across 60 published Power BI reports, there are 45 separate semantic models, many of them near-duplicates built by individual analysts pulling from the same source tables with slightly different measure logic. New reports routinely start from a copy of an existing .pbix rather than connecting to a shared dataset, because that's faster for the analyst and nobody stopped them. Propose an architecture and a governance mechanism that gets the organization to a smaller number of reused, trustworthy semantic models without halting report delivery for months.
questions.modelAnswer: The architecture is a small set of shared, centrally-owned semantic models per subject area (sales, finance, operations) published to their own workspaces, with reports connecting live via "Connect to a Power BI semantic model" rather than importing their own copy. To make that the easy path instead of the slow one, I'd use endorsement: promote the handful of models that should be the standard to Certified, which signals trust in the model hub and discoverability search, and reserve Promoted for departmental models that are useful but not yet canonical. I wouldn't try to retire all 45 models at once; I'd identify the two or three most-duplicated subject areas, consolidate those into certified shared models first, and migrate the highest-traffic reports onto them, proving the reuse pattern works before tackling the long tail. For new report requests, I'd change the default workflow so analysts are pointed at the certified model catalog first, with a lightweight exception process (and manager sign-off) required to build a new model, which removes the silent "copy a pbix" default without needing to police every request. I'd also expose the XMLA endpoint so power users who need deeper model access use Tabular Editor or Analyze in Excel against the shared model instead of fragmenting a new one.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by asking why analysts default to copying a pbix instead of connecting to a shared model, because if that's genuinely the fastest path today, no policy memo is going to change behavior — I have to make the governed path the fast path. So architecturally, I'd consolidate toward a small number of certified, centrally-owned semantic models per subject area, living in their own workspaces, with reports connecting live instead of importing. Certification matters here specifically because it's the signal that tells an analyst 'start here' when they're searching the model hub, instead of guessing which of 45 models is trustworthy. I wouldn't try to boil the ocean — I'd pick the one or two subject areas with the worst duplication, build the certified model, and actively migrate the highest-traffic reports onto it as a proof point, both for trust and for momentum. For new work going forward, I'd change the default workflow itself: point people at the model catalog first and require a sign-off to spin up a net-new model, so the fragmentation stops happening by default rather than by enforcement. And for the power users who were duplicating models because they needed deeper access, I'd open up the XMLA endpoint so they get what they need against the shared model instead of forking their own.
commonMistakes: Mandating consolidation without changing the default workflow that caused the duplication in the first place
Attempting to retire all duplicate models simultaneously instead of targeting the worst offenders first
Not using endorsement (Certified/Promoted) to signal which model is the trustworthy source
Forcing all report authors onto live connections without addressing power users' need for deeper model access (XMLA)
Treating this as a one-time cleanup project rather than an ongoing governance process with an exception path
Ignoring that "faster for the analyst" is the root cause, not analyst carelessness
keyPoints: Small set of certified, centrally-owned semantic models per subject area, connected to live rather than imported
Use of endorsement (Certified vs. Promoted) to drive discoverability and trust
Phased consolidation starting with the most-duplicated subject areas
Default-workflow change (catalog-first, exception process) rather than pure policy enforcement
XMLA endpoint access for power users to avoid new fragmentation
A sustainable governance process rather than a one-time cleanup

Realistic phased consolidation approach
Addresses root cause via default-workflow change, not just policy
Accounts for power-user needs (XMLA) without reintroducing fragmentation

questions.title: Git-Based Version Control and CI/CD for a Power BI Team
questions.prompt: Your Power BI team of 10 analysts has no version control: every change lives inside binary .pbix files, nobody can diff what changed between versions, and two analysts once overwrote each other's work on the same report in the same afternoon. You're asked to design a Git-based workflow and promotion pipeline for the team's Power BI content that gives real version history and code review, not just file backups. What do you propose, and what are the real constraints you have to work around?
questions.modelAnswer: The core move is adopting the Power BI Project (.pbip) format with TMDL for the semantic model, which serializes the report and model as readable text/metadata files instead of a single binary, making them meaningfully diffable and mergeable in Git — this is the real enabler; without it, "Git for Power BI" is just binary file storage with extra steps. I'd set up a repo per domain's content, branch-per-change workflow, and require pull requests with at least one reviewer before merging to main, which gives the code-review step the team is missing today. For promotion, I'd pair Git with Power BI deployment pipelines rather than replacing them: Git becomes the source of truth and review gate for changes, and deployment pipelines (or a scripted deployment via the REST API/Fabric APIs for teams wanting full CI/CD) handle promoting the validated artifact through Dev/Test/Prod workspaces. The constraint to call out honestly is that not everything is perfectly diffable even in .pbip/TMDL — visual-layer layout changes can still produce noisy diffs, and some legacy content may need to be rebuilt in the new format rather than converted automatically. I'd pilot this with one willing team, document the branching and PR conventions, and only mandate it org-wide once the workflow is proven, rather than forcing a format migration on every analyst simultaneously.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by naming why 'put the pbix in a folder in Git' doesn't actually solve this team's problem — it's a binary blob, so you get version history but no diffs and no real code review, which is exactly what they're missing. The real fix is moving to the .pbip/TMDL project format, because that's what turns a Power BI report and model into text-based files Git can actually reason about. Once that's in place, I'd put a normal engineering workflow on top: branches, pull requests, at least one reviewer before merge, so the afternoon-overwrite problem goes away because people are working in their own branches, not the same live file. I wouldn't throw out deployment pipelines, though — Git handles the review and change-history side, and pipelines still do the job of promoting a validated change through Dev, Test, and Prod. I'd be upfront with the team that this isn't a flip-a-switch migration: some existing content will need to be rebuilt in the new format, and even with TMDL, visual layout changes can still generate messy diffs that take some getting used to. So I'd pilot it with one or two analysts who are bought in, nail down our branching and review conventions with them, and only roll it out to the full team once we've worked out the rough edges.
commonMistakes: Assuming putting .pbix files into a Git repo alone solves the problem, without adopting .pbip/TMDL
Designing a Git workflow that replaces deployment pipelines instead of working alongside them for environment promotion
Mandating the new format and workflow for the entire team on day one instead of piloting it
Not establishing a PR/review requirement, missing the actual "code review" gap the team needs fixed
Overselling diff quality — ignoring that visual-layer changes can still produce noisy diffs even in TMDL
No plan for migrating or rebuilding legacy .pbix content into the new project format
keyPoints: Adoption of .pbip/TMDL as the enabler of real diffs and merges in Git
Branch-per-change workflow with mandatory pull request review
Git as source-of-truth/review gate paired with deployment pipelines for environment promotion
Honest acknowledgment of diff/format limitations and legacy-content migration effort
Pilot-then-rollout approach rather than a forced day-one migration
Clear statement of what problem is actually being solved (review + diffability, not just backup)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies .pbip/TMDL as the technical enabler
Sound Git workflow design (branching, PR review)
Correct integration with deployment pipelines rather than replacing them
Realistic rollout plan and honest constraints

questions.title: Orchestration Architecture for Data Landing a Power BI Semantic Layer
questions.prompt: A Power BI semantic model that executives check every morning depends on an Azure Data Factory pipeline that lands and transforms source data overnight. Twice in the last quarter, the Power BI scheduled refresh ran against partially-landed data because an upstream Data Factory pipeline was still running or had silently failed, and nobody noticed until a VP saw wrong numbers. Design the orchestration architecture that connects the Data Factory pipeline to the Power BI refresh so this class of failure can't recur silently.
questions.modelAnswer: The root issue is that the Power BI refresh schedule and the Data Factory pipeline schedule are two independent clocks with no dependency enforced between them, so "ran at 6am" is being used as a proxy for "data is ready," which is unreliable. The fix is to make the Power BI refresh event-driven off pipeline completion rather than time-driven: trigger the dataset refresh from the Data Factory pipeline's success path, using the Power BI REST API (or a Power Automate flow) called as the final step of the pipeline, only after validation activities confirm row counts, freshness timestamps, or a completeness check against the landed data. If the pipeline fails or the validation check fails, that final step simply doesn't fire, and the previous day's data stays in the report rather than silently refreshing against a partial load — which is strictly better than a wrong number appearing with no signal. I'd pair that with alerting on both ends: a Data Factory alert on pipeline failure routed to the data engineering on-call, and a Power BI data-driven alert or a simple "last successful refresh timestamp" visual on the report itself so executives (and the BI team) can see when the data is stale at a glance rather than trusting it blindly. This turns an invisible failure mode into a visible one on both the engineering side and the consumption side.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by naming the actual bug in the architecture: refresh-on-a-timer assumes the upstream pipeline always finishes on time, and twice this quarter it didn't, so the fix isn't a later refresh time, it's removing the assumption. I'd move to event-driven refresh — have the Data Factory pipeline call the Power BI refresh itself, as its last step, only after it's confirmed success and run some kind of data-quality or completeness check. That way a failed or still-running pipeline just means the refresh doesn't happen, and the dashboard shows yesterday's numbers instead of silently wrong ones — stale is a much safer failure mode than wrong. I'd also make sure failure is loud, not quiet: a Data Factory alert that pages engineering when the pipeline fails, and on the Power BI side, something as simple as a last-refreshed timestamp visible on the report itself, so if someone's looking at the dashboard and the data's a day old, they can see that immediately instead of a VP finding out by noticing the numbers look wrong. The bigger principle I'd carry into the conversation with leadership is that 'it ran' was never the right signal to trust — 'it ran, succeeded, and passed a sanity check' is, and that's the behavior change this incident should drive.
commonMistakes: Treating the refresh schedule's run time as proof that upstream data is ready
No dependency link between the Data Factory pipeline's success state and the Power BI refresh trigger
No data-quality/completeness validation step before triggering refresh
No failure alerting on the Data Factory side routed to an accountable owner
No visible freshness indicator on the report itself for consumers to self-check
Fixing this by just moving the refresh time later instead of removing the time-based assumption
keyPoints: Event-driven refresh triggered by pipeline success rather than a fixed time schedule
Validation/completeness checks before the refresh trigger fires
Use of Power BI REST API or Power Automate to connect pipeline completion to refresh
Alerting on pipeline failure to an accountable engineering owner
Visible freshness/last-refresh indicator for report consumers
Preference for a stale-but-correct failure mode over a fresh-but-wrong one

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the time-based dependency flaw
Designs an event-driven, validated trigger mechanism
Includes alerting and freshness visibility for both engineering and consumers
Recommendation avoids a merely cosmetic fix (e.g. just rescheduling)

questions.title: Design Review: Splitting a Monolithic dbt Project Into a dbt Mesh
questions.prompt: Six domain teams (Finance, Sales, Marketing, Product, Ops, Support) currently all commit to one dbt project with 900+ models, built on a single shared Snowflake account. You're asked to design the migration to a dbt Mesh architecture. Walk through the domain boundaries you'd draw, the public/private model decisions, how ownership and CI/CD change, and the biggest risk in the migration itself.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd start from data lineage, not org chart: pull the existing DAG and cluster models by which source systems and which downstream consumers actually touch them, because the real domain boundaries are usually close to but not identical to team names — a 'Sales' model heavily consumed by Finance's commission calculations might belong better owned jointly or by whichever team can actually guarantee its stability. For each resulting domain project, I'd classify every model as public (intentionally exposed, gets a contract and a stable owner committed to not breaking it casually), protected (used only within that project, free to change), or private (truly internal, implementation detail) — the goal being to minimize the public surface area, since every public model is a long-term support commitment. Each domain gets its own dbt project, its own CI pipeline, its own deploy cadence, and its own on-call ownership, with cross-project ref() replacing what used to be same-project ref() for the genuinely shared models; this means each team can now ship on their own schedule without waiting on a shared PR queue, but it also means the platform team's job shifts from 'review every PR' to 'own the mesh conventions, the contract/versioning discipline, and the shared Snowflake account's warehouse/cost governance across all six projects.' The biggest risk is undercounting hidden cross-domain dependencies — models nobody flagged as 'shared' because they were being ref()'d silently within the one big project — so before cutting anything over, I'd generate a full lineage map of which models are actually ref()'d from outside their intended domain and treat every one of those as a required public model with a contract, not an afterthought discovered when a team's build breaks post-migration.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell leadership this is two projects wearing one name: a repo-splitting project and a governance project, and the governance half is where the real risk lives. Technically, clustering models by actual lineage rather than org chart is the right starting point, and I'd deliberately keep the public surface small on day one — it's much easier to promote a protected model to public later than to walk back a public contract six teams have already built on. The part I'd flag loudest as a risk is hidden cross-domain ref()s that nobody documented because they didn't need to in a single shared project; I'd insist on running a full lineage audit before cutover, because finding those after the split means a team's first day on the new architecture is a broken build, which kills trust in the whole initiative.
commonMistakes: Draws domain boundaries purely along the org chart without checking actual data lineage and cross-team dependencies
Makes too many models public by default 'just in case', creating unnecessary long-term contract maintenance burden
Doesn't audit for hidden/undocumented cross-domain ref()s before cutting over
Treats this as purely a technical repo-split without addressing the ownership and CI/CD governance changes
keyPoints: Draws domain boundaries from actual lineage/dependency analysis, not just team names
Deliberately minimizes public model surface area, defaulting to protected/private
Describes the shift in platform team role from PR gatekeeping to mesh governance and shared cost/warehouse oversight
Identifies hidden cross-domain dependencies as the primary migration risk, requiring a pre-cutover lineage audit

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Sound domain-boundary methodology based on lineage, not just org chart
Correct public/protected/private model strategy with sound reasoning
Describes the organizational/governance shift accurately
Identifies and mitigates the hidden-dependency migration risk

questions.title: Design Review: Multi-Warehouse Strategy and Cost Governance for 500+ Snowflake Users
questions.prompt: A 500-person company is scaling Snowflake usage fast: ELT jobs, 40 Power BI dashboards, and a growing group of analysts running ad hoc queries all currently share two large, always-on warehouses, and nobody can say which team's workload drives the bill. Design the multi-warehouse strategy and cost-governance structure you'd put in place.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd split by workload shape, not by team, because the thing that actually determines the right warehouse size and auto-suspend setting is query pattern, not org chart: a small, tightly auto-suspended (60-second) warehouse for scheduled ELT jobs, since those are predictable, batchable, and shouldn't idle; a medium multi-cluster warehouse sized for concurrency (not raw size) for BI dashboard queries, since the real BI bottleneck is usually many simultaneous short queries, not any single query's complexity, and multi-cluster scaling handles concurrent load better than a single larger warehouse; and a separate, deliberately smaller ad hoc/analyst warehouse with its own resource monitor and a short auto-suspend, since exploratory queries are the least predictable and most likely source of a runaway cost surprise. Each warehouse gets its own resource monitor with a quota appropriate to its workload, and critically, each warehouse's naming and tagging scheme maps to a cost center so WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY can actually attribute spend by team/workload instead of one undifferentiated number. I'd also set an account-level resource monitor as a hard backstop across everything. The governance structure on top: a monthly cost review using ACCOUNT_USAGE data broken down by warehouse, a lightweight approval process for anyone wanting a new always-on warehouse or a warehouse size increase, and documentation of which team owns which warehouse's budget — because the technical isolation only pays off if someone's actually accountable for each warehouse's spend trend.
questions.professionalAnswer: My pitch to leadership would be: right now you literally cannot answer 'which team is spending our Snowflake budget,' and that's the actual problem, not the total number. Splitting by workload shape — ELT, BI, ad hoc — each on its own appropriately-sized warehouse with its own auto-suspend and its own resource monitor, gives us that visibility for free as a side effect of doing warehouse sizing correctly in the first place. I'd specifically push back on sizing the BI warehouse larger when the real issue is concurrency, not query complexity — multi-cluster scaling is the right lever there, not warehouse size. And I'd insist on a monthly review cadence against ACCOUNT_USAGE data with named owners per warehouse, because isolation without an owner just becomes three warehouses nobody's watching instead of two.
commonMistakes: Splits warehouses by team/department rather than by actual workload shape and query pattern
Sizes the BI warehouse up for concurrency instead of using multi-cluster scaling
Proposes isolation without a cost-attribution/tagging scheme, so spend still can't be broken down afterward
Proposes resource monitors without an ongoing review cadence or named ownership
keyPoints: Splits warehouses by workload shape (ELT, BI concurrency, ad hoc) rather than by org chart
Uses multi-cluster scaling for BI concurrency rather than oversizing a single warehouse
Sets per-warehouse resource monitors plus an account-level backstop
Establishes a cost-attribution/tagging scheme and a recurring review cadence with named ownership

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct workload-based warehouse segmentation strategy
Correctly distinguishes concurrency (multi-cluster) from raw size needs
Resource monitor strategy at both warehouse and account level
Proposes ongoing cost-attribution and governance cadence
