questions.title: Design Review: The dbt + Airflow + Snowflake Platform, End to End
questions.prompt: You're designing the orchestration architecture for a new analytics platform from scratch: Snowflake as the warehouse, dbt for transformation, and Airflow for orchestration. Walk through how the three fit together, what Airflow should and shouldn't be responsible for relative to dbt, and how you'd structure the DAGs so the platform scales as more domain teams add their own dbt models.
questions.modelAnswer: The division of responsibility I'd design for: Airflow owns scheduling, cross-system dependencies, and operational concerns (retries, alerting, SLAs, waiting on external systems via sensors/deferrable operators), while dbt owns the actual transformation DAG — model-to-model dependencies, materialization strategy, testing, and documentation — and Airflow should not try to re-implement or micromanage dbt's internal dependency graph. Concretely, I'd have Airflow trigger dbt at a reasonably coarse grain (a `dbt build` or a dbt Cloud job trigger for a tagged selection of models, not one Airflow task per dbt model), because dbt already resolves its own internal ordering correctly and splitting that into hundreds of individual Airflow tasks just duplicates dependency logic in two places and makes Airflow's DAG enormous and fragile. For a platform where multiple domain teams add their own dbt projects (in a mesh pattern) over time, I'd give each domain its own Airflow DAG that triggers its own dbt project's build, with cross-domain ordering handled via Dataset-based scheduling (each dbt project's Airflow DAG declares the Snowflake tables/marts it produces as datasets; a downstream domain's DAG schedules off those datasets) rather than a single mega-DAG trying to orchestrate every team's models centrally — that keeps each team's pipeline independently deployable and failure-isolated, so Marketing's dbt build failing doesn't block Finance's DAG from running. Airflow's job here is being the connective tissue and operational safety net between domains, not the owner of transformation logic.
questions.professionalAnswer: The design principle I'd lead with: dbt already knows how its own models depend on each other, so Airflow's job is not to re-derive that, it's to decide when to run dbt and what to do if it fails. I'd trigger dbt at the project or tagged-selection level from Airflow, not model-by-model, and for a mesh of multiple domain teams, I'd give each domain its own DAG triggering its own dbt project, connected to each other via Datasets rather than one giant orchestrator DAG that becomes a single point of fragility for every team. If someone proposes an Airflow task per dbt model, my answer is that's duplicating a dependency graph dbt already solved, and it makes the Airflow DAG the hardest thing in the system to reason about for no benefit.
commonMistakes: Proposes one Airflow task per dbt model, duplicating dbt's own dependency resolution unnecessarily
Has Airflow try to manage dbt's internal model-to-model ordering instead of triggering dbt at a coarser grain
Proposes a single centralized mega-DAG for all domains instead of per-domain DAGs connected via Datasets
Doesn't clearly separate Airflow's operational role (retries, alerting, cross-system waits) from dbt's transformation role
keyPoints: Clearly separates Airflow's orchestration/operational role from dbt's transformation-DAG ownership
Triggers dbt at a coarse grain (project/tagged selection), not one Airflow task per model
Uses per-domain DAGs connected via Dataset-based scheduling rather than one mega-DAG, for a multi-team mesh
Explains the failure-isolation benefit of per-domain DAGs

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly separates Airflow's and dbt's respective responsibilities
Recommends coarse-grained dbt triggering rather than per-model Airflow tasks
Designs per-domain DAGs with Dataset-based cross-domain ordering
Explains the failure-isolation and scalability benefits clearly

questions.title: Design Review: Rolling Out a dbt Semantic Layer as the Single Source of Truth
questions.prompt: Leadership wants every KPI used in executive reporting to come from exactly one place, after a quarter of conflicting numbers across Power BI, ad hoc SQL, and a data science team's notebooks. Design the rollout of a dbt Semantic Layer to actually achieve this, including how you'd handle the existing reports that already exist outside it.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd start narrow and prove the model before going wide: pick the two or three KPIs that caused the actual conflicts last quarter, define them once as dbt metrics with their semantic models, and migrate just the reports that use those specific KPIs first — not because the rest doesn't matter, but because a narrow, successful pilot with a believable before/after story ('these three numbers used to disagree, now they don't, here's why') is what actually gets the next round of teams to cooperate. For the architecture itself: each KPI's semantic model declares its entities, dimensions, and measures once in dbt; BI tools connect via the Semantic Layer's API/connector rather than querying marts directly, and I'd explicitly request (with executive backing) that direct mart access for those specific tables be restricted or at least flagged in a data catalog as 'not the source of truth for this metric' so new reports don't accidentally bypass the layer. For existing reports built before the Semantic Layer existed, I'd inventory every report currently showing one of the migrated KPIs (this requires some manual discovery, since there's no perfect automated way to find every SQL query hitting a mart table across every tool), prioritize migration by how business-critical and how frequently viewed each report is, and set a firm deprecation date for the old underlying queries once migration is confirmed — a 'soft' migration with no deprecation date for the old path just means the conflicting numbers come back the next time someone forks an old report.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd resist the urge to migrate everything at once. Pick the KPIs that actually caused last quarter's pain, define them once, migrate the specific reports that use them, and get a clean before/after story — that's what builds the credibility to ask five more teams to give up their local definitions. The part I'd be most insistent on with leadership is the deprecation step: migrating three reports to the Semantic Layer while leaving ten other reports still querying the raw tables directly doesn't actually solve the conflicting-numbers problem, it just adds a fourth source of truth. I'd ask for executive backing specifically to set and enforce a deprecation date on the old direct-query path for each migrated KPI, because that's the part that requires authority I don't have on my own.
commonMistakes: Proposes migrating every KPI and every report simultaneously instead of a narrow, provable pilot
Doesn't address what happens to existing reports built before the Semantic Layer existed
Treats the rollout as complete once the metric is defined, without restricting or deprecating the old direct-query path
Doesn't ask for executive backing to actually deprecate old paths, which requires authority beyond the analytics engineering team
keyPoints: Starts with a narrow pilot on the specific KPIs that caused real conflicts, not a full migration at once
Describes the Semantic Layer architecture (semantic models, measures, API/connector access)
Inventories and prioritizes migration of existing reports built outside the Semantic Layer
Requires executive-backed deprecation of old direct-query paths as the step that actually prevents drift from returning

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a sound, narrow pilot-first rollout strategy
Correctly describes the Semantic Layer architecture and access pattern
Addresses migrating/inventorying existing pre-existing reports
Identifies deprecation of old paths (with executive backing) as essential to prevent recurrence

questions.title: Design Review: Multi-Tenant Airflow for Eight Independent Teams
questions.prompt: Eight engineering teams want to run their own DAGs on a shared Airflow deployment, but leadership is worried about one team's bad DAG (an infinite retry loop, a resource-hungry task) degrading the platform for everyone else. Design the multi-tenancy strategy — pools, queues, DAG-level resource limits, and ownership boundaries — that makes shared Airflow safe at this scale.
questions.modelAnswer: The core tool for blast-radius containment is pools: I'd give each team its own pool with a slot limit sized to their actual workload, so a runaway DAG from one team can only ever consume that team's own pool slots, not starve the other seven teams' tasks of worker capacity — without pools, every team's tasks compete for the same global worker slots, and one team's misbehaving DAG genuinely can degrade everyone. On top of pools, I'd set per-DAG defaults for max_active_runs and a hard default_task_retries ceiling (teams can request an exception, but the default prevents an infinite-retry-loop DAG from hammering the metadata database or an external system indefinitely), and I'd use execution queues/worker pools (in Celery/Kubernetes executor terms) to physically separate resource-hungry workloads (e.g., a team running heavy Spark-submitting tasks) from lightweight ones, so a resource-hungry task type doesn't get scheduled onto the same worker capacity as time-sensitive, lightweight DAGs. For ownership boundaries, each team would own their own DAG files/repo folder with CI that validates their DAGs against baseline guardrails (reasonable retry limits, required tags, required owner contact) before merge, with the platform team owning the shared Airflow infrastructure itself (scheduler, metadata DB, triggerer) and the cross-cutting guardrails, not reviewing every team's DAG logic line by line. I'd also set DAG-level SLAs and alerting routed to each team's own on-call, so a team's bad DAG pages them first, not the platform team.
questions.professionalAnswer: The one thing that actually prevents 'one team's bad DAG degrades everyone' is pools — give each team a slot allocation that caps how much of the shared worker capacity they can ever consume, full stop. I'd pair that with a default retry ceiling and max_active_runs setting that teams can't exceed without an explicit platform-approved exception, specifically to prevent an infinite-retry DAG from quietly hammering the metadata database for days. For ownership, I'd draw a hard line: the platform team owns the shared infrastructure and the baseline guardrails enforced in CI, each team owns their own DAG logic and is the first page when their DAG misbehaves. I'd present this to leadership as: multi-tenancy isn't 'trust everyone to write good DAGs,' it's 'make it structurally impossible for one team's mistake to be everyone else's incident.'
commonMistakes: Relies on code review/trust alone instead of pools as the actual technical containment mechanism
Doesn't set default retry/max_active_runs ceilings, leaving a path open for an infinite-retry DAG to degrade shared infrastructure
Doesn't separate resource-hungry task types onto their own queues/worker pools
Makes the platform team responsible for reviewing every team's DAG logic instead of owning shared infrastructure and baseline guardrails
keyPoints: Uses per-team pools as the primary blast-radius containment mechanism
Sets default retry ceilings and max_active_runs limits to prevent runaway resource consumption
Separates resource-hungry workloads onto distinct queues/worker pools
Draws a clear ownership line: platform team owns shared infra and guardrails, each team owns their own DAG logic and on-call

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly proposes pools as the primary containment mechanism
Proposes default retry/concurrency ceilings to prevent runaway resource use
Addresses resource-hungry workload isolation via queues/worker pools
Defines a clear, workable ownership boundary between platform and team roles

questions.title: Design Review: A Cost-Governance Framework Finance Can Actually Audit
questions.prompt: Finance wants more than a resource monitor — they want a repeatable, auditable cost-governance framework for Snowflake spend that they can review quarterly without needing an engineer to explain it each time. Design that framework.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd design this around three layers: prevention, attribution, and review. Prevention is the resource monitor structure already in place (per-warehouse quotas plus an account-level backstop) — necessary but not what finance actually asked for. Attribution is the piece that makes this auditable without an engineer in the room: every warehouse is tagged (via Snowflake object tagging) with a cost-center and an owning team, so a query against ACCOUNT_USAGE.WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY joined to the tag metadata produces a self-service, per-team monthly credit breakdown that finance can pull themselves, rather than a number someone has to translate for them. On top of that, I'd build a standing dashboard (in whatever BI tool finance already uses) sourced from that same attribution query, refreshed daily, so 'quarterly review' becomes looking at twelve months of a trend line rather than someone compiling a report from scratch each quarter. The review layer is a lightweight governance process: any new always-on warehouse or warehouse size increase above a defined threshold requires a brief written justification logged somewhere finance can see (even a simple ticket field), and the quarterly review itself becomes finance looking at the trend dashboard, flagging any team whose spend grew disproportionately to their stated roadmap, and asking that team to explain it directly — not asking engineering to explain everyone's spend on their behalf. The design principle throughout is: every dollar of Snowflake spend should trace to a tagged warehouse, a named owning team, and (for anything unusual) a logged justification, with none of that requiring an engineer's interpretation at review time.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell finance directly: a resource monitor caps spend, it doesn't explain it, and what you're actually asking for is attribution plus a repeatable review process. The fix is tagging every warehouse with a cost center and owner so the metering data already answers 'who's spending what' without translation, building that into a dashboard you can open yourself rather than requesting from engineering each quarter, and adding a lightweight approval/justification step for anything that would meaningfully move the number (a new always-on warehouse, a size bump). Then your quarterly review becomes you looking at a trend line and asking the one team whose number jumped to explain it — which is a conversation you can have directly with them, without me in the room.
commonMistakes: Treats a resource monitor as sufficient for finance's actual ask (an auditable, self-service framework)
Doesn't propose warehouse tagging/cost-center attribution, leaving spend unexplainable without engineering translation
Doesn't propose a standing, finance-owned dashboard, implying a manual report each quarter instead
Doesn't add a lightweight justification/approval step for meaningful spend-increasing changes
keyPoints: Separates prevention (resource monitors), attribution (tagging + ACCOUNT_USAGE), and review (process) as distinct layers
Uses warehouse tagging by cost-center/owner to make spend self-service attributable
Proposes a standing, finance-accessible dashboard rather than a manual quarterly report
Adds a lightweight justification/approval step for significant spend-increasing changes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes prevention, attribution, and review as separate needs
Proposes a concrete tagging/attribution mechanism
Proposes a self-service dashboard rather than a manual report
Proposes a lightweight, enforceable justification/approval process

questions.title: Design Review: Migration Path From One dbt Project to dbt Mesh, Without a Flag Day
questions.prompt: You've decided dbt Mesh is right for a 400-model project splitting across four teams, but the business has made clear there's no acceptable window for a 'big bang' cutover — reporting can't go down. Design the incremental migration path from the current single project to the target multi-project mesh.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd migrate one domain at a time, starting with the domain that has the fewest and most well-understood cross-domain dependencies, rather than the most urgent or most visible one, so the first migration is the lowest-risk proof of the process. For that domain: extract its models into a new, separate dbt project while temporarily keeping the old project's copies in place (even if now unused by the extracted team), declare the extracted project's shared models as public with contracts, and have the remaining monolith project's models that depend on the extracted domain switch their ref()s to cross-project references pointing at the new project — this can be done model by model, verified by comparing output row counts/values between the old in-project version and the new cross-project version before fully cutting over, so there's a verification step rather than a leap of faith. Only once the new cross-project references are confirmed matching and stable would I remove the now-redundant copies from the monolith. I'd repeat this domain by domain, each one validated independently, rather than attempting to extract all four domains simultaneously, specifically because that lets any issue surface and get fixed within one domain's blast radius instead of blocking the whole migration. The sequencing also matters for team morale and buy-in — a successful first domain migration with zero reporting disruption is the evidence that makes the next team willing to go through the same process.
questions.professionalAnswer: No flag day means no simultaneous four-way split — I'd do this one domain at a time, starting with whichever domain has the cleanest, most understood dependencies, specifically so the first migration is a low-risk proof point rather than our hardest case. The verification step I'd insist on for each model being extracted: run the old in-project version and the new cross-project version side by side and diff the output before removing the old copy, so we're never relying on 'it should be equivalent' without checking. I'd tell the business this means the full migration takes longer than a big-bang approach would, but the tradeoff is explicitly zero reporting downtime and a much smaller blast radius if anything goes wrong with any single domain's extraction.
commonMistakes: Proposes extracting all four domains simultaneously despite the explicit no-flag-day constraint
Removes the old monolith copies before verifying the new cross-project references produce matching output
Starts with the most urgent/visible domain rather than the lowest-risk one for the first proof-of-process migration
Doesn't propose a concrete verification step (output comparison) between old and new references
keyPoints: Migrates one domain at a time rather than attempting a simultaneous multi-domain split
Starts with the lowest-risk domain as a proof point before tackling harder domains
Keeps old in-project copies temporarily and verifies output parity before removing them
Explains the tradeoff of a longer timeline in exchange for zero reporting downtime and smaller blast radius

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a sound incremental, domain-by-domain migration sequence
Includes a concrete verification/parity-check step before cutover
Justifies starting with the lowest-risk domain, not the most urgent
Clearly communicates the timeline/risk tradeoff to the business

questions.title: Leading the incident bridge: RLS exposed the wrong region's data
questions.prompt: A regional manager reports they can see another region's sales figures in a production dashboard that's supposed to be restricted by dynamic RLS. This is a real data-exposure incident, not a bug report. Walk through how you lead the incident response in the first hour, and what you do differently afterward.
questions.modelAnswer: In the first hour, containment comes before root-causing. I'd immediately check whether the affected workspace/report can be pulled from general access or the semantic model's access temporarily restricted while we investigate — stopping further exposure matters more than understanding it in the first ten minutes. In parallel, I'd scope the blast radius with specific questions, not vague ones: which users are affected, is it one region seeing one other region or a broader leak, and is this isolated to one report or does it affect every report on the same semantic model (Lesson 83's note that RLS filters the whole semantic model, not one page, makes this a real question to answer, not assume). Root-cause candidates I'd check in order, because they're the documented failure modes: is the affected user actually a workspace Viewer, or did they get promoted to Contributor/Member at some point, since RLS silently doesn't apply above Viewer; does the user-mapping table's UPN format actually match what USERPRINCIPALNAME() returns in the service, since Desktop and service can format identity differently; and is a bidirectional-filtering relationship change or a recent model republish the likely trigger, checking recent publish history for timing correlation. I'd communicate status honestly and promptly to the affected manager and to leadership — what we know, what we don't yet, and what's been contained — rather than going quiet until we have a full answer, since a data-exposure incident that looks like silence looks worse than one being actively managed. Afterward: a written incident review covering exact root cause, why Test as role (or whatever validation step existed) didn't catch it, and a concrete process fix — likely requiring Test as role validation as a mandatory, logged gate before any RLS-affecting change reaches production, not an optional best practice. I'd also push for periodic re-validation of RLS roles, not just at initial build, since workspace role creep (a Viewer quietly promoted to Contributor) is exactly the kind of drift that goes unnoticed until an incident surfaces it.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move isn't diagnosis, it's containment — can we restrict access to that report or semantic model right now while we figure out what happened, because stopping the exposure matters more in minute ten than understanding it does. Once that's moving, I scope it precisely: who's affected, is this one leaked region or several, and does it touch every report on this semantic model or just one — because RLS applies at the semantic-model level, so I treat 'just one report' as a question to verify, not an assumption. Then I work the known failure modes in order, because this isn't the first time anyone's hit these: is the affected person actually a Viewer, or did they get bumped to Contributor at some point and RLS silently stopped applying to them; does our mapping table's email format actually match what the service returns for USERPRINCIPALNAME, because that mismatch is the single most common reason dynamic RLS misbehaves; and did something change recently — a republish, a relationship edit — that lines up with when this started. I keep the affected manager and leadership updated honestly as I go, even with partial information, because silence during a data exposure reads worse than an honest 'here's what we know so far.' Afterward, the real deliverable isn't just the fix — it's making sure Test as role, or whatever validation step should have caught this, becomes a mandatory, logged gate before anything RLS-related ships again, and that we're periodically re-checking role assignments, because a Viewer quietly becoming a Contributor is exactly the kind of drift nobody notices until it's an incident.
commonMistakes: Starting with root-cause investigation before containing further exposure
Assuming the leak is isolated to one report without checking the whole semantic model
Not checking the affected user's actual workspace role first (Viewer vs Contributor/Member)
Going quiet during the incident instead of communicating partial findings honestly
Treating the fix as complete without adding a mandatory pre-production validation gate afterward
keyPoints: Containment precedes root-causing in a real data-exposure incident
RLS applies at the semantic-model level — check all reports on that model, not just the one reported
Check whether the affected user is actually a Viewer; role promotion silently defeats RLS
UPN/email format mismatch between Desktop and service is a documented, common root cause
Post-incident fix must include a mandatory validation gate and periodic role re-checks, not just a patch

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Prioritizes containment before full root-cause investigation
Methodically checks the documented RLS failure modes (role level, UPN format, model-wide scope)
Describes honest, timely stakeholder communication during the incident
Proposes a concrete post-incident process fix, not just a one-time patch

questions.title: Negotiating a Shared Definition of 'Revenue' Between Finance and Sales Leadership
questions.prompt: Finance and Sales leadership both want their own definition of 'Revenue' baked into the same shared semantic model -- Finance wants recognized revenue net of returns and allowances, Sales wants booked revenue at the time of sale. Both insist their number is 'the' revenue number, and both want it labeled simply 'Revenue' with no qualifier. As the architect, how do you resolve this?
questions.modelAnswer: I would not try to arbitrate which definition is 'more correct' -- both are legitimate, well-understood business metrics that answer different real questions, and my job isn't to tell Finance or Sales their definition is wrong. The actual problem is the naming collision, not the metrics themselves: two different, equally valid numbers cannot both be called 'Revenue' with no qualifier in the same model, because every report built afterward inherits that ambiguity and nobody downstream will know which 'Revenue' they're looking at. I'd bring both groups into the same room, show them concretely what happens when an executive pulls up two dashboards built on the same model and sees two different 'Revenue' figures with identical labels -- this isn't hypothetical, it's the standard failure mode that erodes trust in the whole platform -- and propose explicit, unambiguous names for both: 'Booked Revenue' and 'Recognized Revenue' as two separate, clearly documented measures, both available in the same model, neither one hidden or treated as secondary. I'd frame this as giving both groups exactly what they need, correctly labeled, rather than making either side give up their number. If there's residual pressure for an unqualified 'Revenue' somewhere in an executive-level report, I'd push for that report to explicitly state which definition it's using in a visible label or footnote, rather than letting an ambiguous default quietly pick a winner. The result I'm protecting is that any future person looking at either number knows exactly what they're looking at, without having to ask.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't try to tell either Finance or Sales that their number is wrong, because it isn't -- booked revenue and recognized revenue are both real, legitimate ways to answer different questions, and arguing about which one deserves the plain word 'Revenue' is actually a naming fight, not a metrics fight. So that's how I'd reframe it to both of them, together, in the same room: the problem isn't your number, it's that if we call two different numbers the same thing in the same model, every dashboard anyone builds from here forward is a trap waiting to show two different 'Revenue' figures with the same label, and that's exactly the kind of thing that makes an executive stop trusting the whole platform. My proposal is always to give both groups exactly what they want, just named precisely -- Booked Revenue, Recognized Revenue, both built, both documented, neither one buried as an afterthought. That usually lands fine, because nobody's actually losing their number, they're just not allowed to call it something that conflicts with someone else's equally valid number anymore.
commonMistakes: Tries to decide which definition is 'correct' instead of recognizing both are legitimate for different purposes
Lets both measures ship under the same ambiguous 'Revenue' label to avoid the conflict
Picks one side's definition to end the argument, alienating the other stakeholder group
Doesn't anticipate or address the downstream risk of two differently-labeled dashboards showing conflicting 'Revenue' figures
Treats this as purely a technical naming fix without actually bringing both stakeholder groups into the conversation
keyPoints: Recognizes both definitions as legitimate rather than trying to arbitrate correctness
Reframes the conflict as a naming/governance problem, not a metrics dispute
Proposes explicit, unambiguous names for both measures, both fully supported
Addresses the downstream risk of ambiguous labeling eroding trust in the platform
Resolves the conflict without requiring either stakeholder group to give up their number

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recognizes both definitions as legitimate rather than picking a winner
Correctly reframes the conflict as a naming/governance issue
Proposes a concrete resolution (explicit naming) that satisfies both stakeholder groups
Addresses the downstream trust risk of ambiguous metric labeling

questions.title: Telling a VP Their Requested Real-Time Dashboard Isn't Feasible on the Current Architecture
questions.prompt: A VP asks for a dashboard that updates in real time as transactions happen. Your current architecture refreshes the semantic model on a scheduled basis and genuinely cannot do sub-second real-time updates without a significant redesign the VP hasn't budgeted for. How do you handle this conversation without just saying no?
questions.modelAnswer: I wouldn't open with 'that's not possible,' because that's technically imprecise and it closes the conversation instead of moving it forward -- what's actually true is that true real-time isn't feasible on the current architecture without a redesign that isn't currently budgeted, which is a very different, more useful statement. My first move is to understand what the VP is actually trying to solve, because 'real time' is often a proxy for a specific pain -- usually 'I'm making decisions on numbers that are too stale,' not literally 'I need sub-second latency.' Once I understand the real need, I'd lay out the honest spectrum of options with their actual cost and latency tradeoffs: the current scheduled refresh (cheap, but however stale the current interval is), a shorter scheduled refresh interval (cheap incremental improvement, still not real-time), DirectQuery against the source for near-real-time numbers at the cost of some query performance and load on the source system, and a genuine real-time architecture (streaming ingestion, a fundamentally different pipeline) that solves the stated request literally but requires a scoped project with its own budget and timeline. I'd recommend whichever point on that spectrum actually matches the business problem the VP described, not necessarily the most technically impressive option, and I'd be explicit that if what they actually need is 'every 15 minutes instead of nightly,' we might be able to deliver real business value cheaply and quickly, without needing the full real-time rebuild they initially asked for by name. This turns 'no' into 'here's what's actually achievable at what cost, and here's what I'd recommend for the problem you're describing,' which gives the VP a real decision to make instead of a wall.
questions.professionalAnswer: I never want to just tell a VP 'no' to this, because it's not actually true and it ends the conversation instead of helping them. What's true is that sub-second real-time isn't something our current architecture does without a redesign nobody's budgeted for -- so instead of leading with the limitation, I lead with a question: what's the actual decision you're trying to make faster, because 'real time' is usually standing in for 'I'm looking at numbers that are too old for what I need to decide,' not literally millisecond freshness. Once I know that, I can lay out the real menu: our current refresh schedule, a tighter refresh interval that's a cheap change, DirectQuery for something close to real-time with a real performance tradeoff on the source system, or an actual real-time pipeline if they genuinely need that and are willing to scope and fund it as its own project. Most of the time, what actually solves their problem is something much cheaper than full real-time, and I'd rather hand them that option clearly than either say no or quietly over-promise something we can't deliver on the current budget.
commonMistakes: Simply says the request isn't possible without exploring what the VP is actually trying to solve
Over-promises real-time capability to avoid an uncomfortable conversation, setting up a later failure
Doesn't present the real spectrum of options (refresh interval, DirectQuery, true real-time) with honest tradeoffs
Recommends the most technically impressive option rather than the one that actually fits the underlying business need
Frames the conversation as a technical limitation rather than a cost/timeline/scope conversation the VP can actually decide on
keyPoints: Avoids a flat 'no,' instead clarifying the real underlying business need behind the request
Presents an honest spectrum of real options with their actual cost/latency tradeoffs
Recommends the option that fits the actual underlying need, not the most impressive-sounding one
Reframes the conversation as a scoped decision the VP can make, not a technical wall
Doesn't over-promise a capability the current architecture can't deliver

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Avoids a flat refusal, instead exploring the VP's actual underlying need
Presents a real, honest spectrum of options with tradeoffs
Recommends an option matched to the real need rather than over- or under-selling
Frames the conversation as a decision for the VP rather than a technical dead end

questions.title: Standardizing on Power BI When a Department Built Its Own Shadow BI System in Excel and Access
questions.prompt: Leadership wants to standardize all BI on Power BI, retiring ad hoc reporting. One department has, over several years, built an elaborate shadow system of linked Excel workbooks and an Access database that they rely on daily and are genuinely attached to. How do you lead the migration of that department without alienating them or losing what actually works about their system?
questions.modelAnswer: The instinct to walk in and declare the shadow system a problem to be eliminated is exactly how this goes wrong -- that system exists and has survived for years because it's actually solving real problems for that department, even if it's also creating real risk (no version control, fragile linked-workbook dependencies, no audit trail, single points of failure if the one person who understands the Access database leaves). My first move is to actually understand what it does well before proposing to replace it: sit with the department, have them walk me through their real workflow, and identify specifically which parts of their process the shadow system is genuinely serving -- flexibility to slice data in ways central tools haven't supported, speed, a sense of ownership over their own numbers -- versus which parts are pure risk with no corresponding benefit. I'd frame the migration explicitly as 'let's build you something that does everything this does, plus removes the risk you're carrying,' not 'stop using what you built because it's against policy.' I'd involve department staff directly in designing the Power BI replacement, specifically because the people who built and maintained the shadow system understand the real business logic buried in those workbooks better than anyone else, and treating them as the experts on their own domain during the build protects their sense of ownership instead of stripping it away. I'd migrate in parallel, not cut over abruptly -- keep the shadow system running until the new Power BI solution has been validated against it for a real stretch of time, so the department never has to trust a new system on faith while their own livelihood depends on the numbers being right. The policy goal (standardize on Power BI) and the department's real need (a system that actually works for their specific workflow) aren't in conflict if I do this right -- they only look like they're in conflict if I lead with the policy instead of the workflow.
questions.professionalAnswer: The mistake I'd be most careful to avoid is walking in and treating their system as the problem, because from their side, it's not a problem -- it's something they built and have relied on for years because it actually works for them, even if it's also a real risk from where I sit. So I start by actually learning it: sit with them, have them walk me through their real day-to-day with it, and figure out specifically what it's doing right for them versus what's just risk with no upside -- no version control, no audit trail, one person who understands the Access database and nobody else. Then I frame the migration as addition, not subtraction: we're building something that does everything their system does for them, and also removes the risk they've been quietly carrying. I bring their own people into designing the Power BI replacement, because they understand the real business logic in those workbooks better than I ever will, and that involvement is also what keeps this from feeling like something being done to them. And I run the two side by side for a real stretch of time rather than cutting over on a deadline, because I'm not going to ask them to trust a new system with numbers their job depends on until it's actually proven itself against the thing they already trust.
commonMistakes: Treats the shadow system as simply wrong or against policy without understanding what it's actually solving for the department
Mandates an abrupt cutover instead of running the new system in parallel until it's proven
Excludes department staff from designing the replacement, losing the real business logic embedded in their existing system
Frames the migration purely as policy compliance rather than addressing the department's real workflow needs
Doesn't acknowledge the genuine risk in the shadow system (no audit trail, single point of failure) as the actual justification for change
keyPoints: Starts by understanding what the shadow system actually does well for the department, not just its risks
Frames the migration as addition (same capability, less risk) rather than pure removal of what they built
Involves department staff directly in designing the replacement to capture real business logic and preserve ownership
Runs the new and old systems in parallel until the replacement is genuinely validated
Balances the organizational governance goal with the department's genuine, legitimate workflow needs

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Understands and respects what the shadow system is actually solving before proposing change
Frames the migration as addition rather than punitive removal
Involves department staff in designing the replacement
Proposes a parallel-run migration rather than an abrupt cutover

questions.title: Prioritizing a Backlog of Competing Dashboard Requests
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you had a large backlog of dashboard and report requests from multiple departments, all claiming urgency. How did you build a prioritization framework and communicate it back to stakeholders?
questions.modelAnswer: The answer should quantify the backlog problem — number of open requests, number of competing departments, and why 'everything is urgent' had become the default. It should describe a concrete prioritization framework rather than ad hoc judgment calls: scoring requests against criteria like business impact, number of downstream decisions affected, cost of delay, and build effort, and making that framework visible to requesters rather than opaque. It should show how the framework was communicated back to stakeholders whose requests ranked lower — specifically how the candidate avoided just disappointing people silently, by explaining the reasoning and giving a realistic timeline. Strong answers mention a lightweight intake and triage process (a backlog board, a regular grooming cadence) so prioritization becomes repeatable rather than a one-time exercise, and close with a measurable outcome: reduced average time-to-delivery, fewer 'why hasn't my request been touched' escalations, or higher stakeholder satisfaction with transparency even when their request wasn't first in line.
questions.professionalAnswer: I inherited a backlog of 47 open dashboard requests across six departments, each department insisting theirs was the most urgent, with no shared criteria for sequencing any of it. I built a simple scoring model with four weighted factors — number of people who'd use it regularly, whether it supported a recurring decision versus a one-off curiosity, estimated build effort, and cost of continuing to delay it — and scored every open request against it in a spreadsheet I made visible to all six department leads, not just my own team. I ran a 30-minute session with each lead to walk through how their specific requests scored and why, which let me say 'your request is real and matters, here's exactly where it lands and why' instead of a vague 'we'll get to it.' Two leads pushed back hard on their ranking, and in one case they were right — I'd underweighted a compliance-driven request from Legal that had a hard regulatory deadline I hadn't accounted for, so I added a deadline-override factor to the model. We moved to a visible Kanban board with a biweekly grooming session so this became routine instead of a one-time fire drill. Average time from request to delivery dropped from eleven weeks to under four, and escalations to my manager about 'my request is stuck' dropped to nearly zero because people could see exactly where they stood and why.
commonMistakes: No concrete scoring criteria, just 'we prioritized based on urgency'
Keeping the prioritization logic opaque instead of sharing it with requesters
Not addressing how deprioritized stakeholders were communicated with
Treating the first prioritization pass as final instead of being open to correction
No repeatable process established, just a one-time cleanup
No measurable improvement in delivery time or stakeholder satisfaction
keyPoints: Quantifies the backlog and the competing-urgency problem
Introduces a concrete, weighted prioritization framework
Makes the framework and resulting rankings visible to stakeholders
Shows willingness to revise the framework when a legitimate gap is found
Establishes a repeatable intake/grooming process, not a one-time fix
Gives a measurable improvement in delivery time or escalation volume

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Concreteness of the prioritization framework
Transparency with stakeholders about rankings and reasoning
Willingness to revise the framework when challenged
Repeatability of the process going forward
Measurable outcome

questions.title: Leading a Platform-Wide Rollout of Naming Conventions and a DAX Style Guide
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you authored and rolled out a platform-wide standard, such as a naming convention, certified dataset tiering system, or DAX style guide, across an entire BI practice. How did you drive adoption?
questions.modelAnswer: The answer should describe the specific standard authored — a naming convention, a certified dataset tiering model, a DAX style guide — and why it was needed at that point (growing team, inconsistent quality, slow onboarding, hard-to-maintain measures). It should show the candidate drafting the standard collaboratively, soliciting input from the analysts who'd actually use it day to day rather than writing it in isolation and imposing it, and piloting it on a real project before declaring it mandatory. It should address enforcement mechanism honestly — a lightweight code-review gate, a linting/checklist step, or a certification review — rather than relying on willpower. It should acknowledge pushback (senior analysts resistant to changing established habits) and how that was handled with patience and clear rationale rather than authority alone. It should close with adoption evidence: percentage of new reports following the standard, reduction in time spent understanding someone else's DAX, or fewer production bugs traced to inconsistent patterns.
questions.professionalAnswer: As our Power BI practice grew from 4 to 14 analysts over a year, every measure was named differently and every analyst had their own DAX style, which meant debugging someone else's report took two or three times longer than it should have. I drafted a first pass of a naming convention and DAX style guide based on patterns from our best-performing existing reports, then sent it to the four most senior analysts for a working review before anyone else saw it, specifically because I knew it would land better coming in partly their language rather than purely mine. We piloted it on one new project for a month, found a few rules that were too rigid in practice — one convention around measure prefixes actually made some of our longer measure names unreadable — and adjusted before rolling it out team-wide. For enforcement, I didn't rely on people just remembering; I added a short pull-request checklist in our Git workflow so any new measure got checked against the style guide before merging, which made it a review-time conversation instead of a retroactive cleanup. Two of our most senior analysts initially found the PR checklist step annoying and said as much directly to me, so I sat down with each of them, walked through a recent debugging session that had taken me 40 minutes because of inconsistent naming, and that concrete example did more to convince them than the style guide document itself. A year later, roughly 90% of our DAX measures followed the convention, and average time to review or extend someone else's report dropped noticeably enough that it came up unprompted in our team retro.
commonMistakes: Writing the standard in isolation and imposing it without analyst input
Rolling it out team-wide immediately with no pilot
Relying on willpower or memory instead of a concrete enforcement mechanism
Dismissing senior analysts' pushback instead of engaging with it directly
No adoption metric or evidence the standard actually took hold
Describing the standard only in the abstract with no specific example of what it contains
keyPoints: Names the specific standard authored and the concrete problem it addressed
Drafts collaboratively with the people who'll use it daily
Pilots before mandating team-wide rollout
Builds a concrete enforcement mechanism, such as a PR/review gate
Engages pushback directly with specific evidence rather than authority
Shows measurable adoption and a resulting efficiency gain

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Specificity of the standard and the problem it solved
Collaborative drafting and piloting approach
Concreteness of the enforcement mechanism
Handling of resistance from senior team members
Measurable adoption outcome

questions.title: Designing a Company-Wide dbt Governance Model Across Competing Teams
questions.prompt: You've been asked to design and get buy-in for a company-wide dbt governance model — naming conventions, testing standards, PR review requirements, and ownership rules — across six teams who currently each run their own dbt practices with no consistency. Several team leads are skeptical this is worth the overhead. Walk through how you'd approach designing and landing this.
questions.modelAnswer: I wouldn't start by writing the standard and asking teams to adopt it — I'd start by pulling concrete pain each team has already experienced from the lack of governance (a broken downstream model from an undocumented change, a metric that disagreed across two teams' dashboards, a new hire who took three weeks to understand a project's structure because every team names things differently) and use those as the actual justification, since skeptical team leads respond to evidence of real cost, not to governance for its own sake. I'd then co-design the standard with a representative from each team rather than writing it unilaterally and presenting it as policy, both because each team has legitimate context the standard needs to accommodate and because co-ownership is what gets voluntary compliance instead of resentful minimum-compliance. I'd deliberately keep the first version narrow — naming conventions and a minimum testing bar, not everything at once — pilot it with one willing team, and use that team's experience (ideally including one caught bug or avoided incident) as the proof point for the next round of adoption, rather than mandating company-wide compliance before anyone's seen it work. For the skeptics specifically, I'd ask what a successful version of 'no governance' actually looks like for their team long-term, which usually surfaces that they're not against standards, they're against standards that don't fit their team's specific constraints — and that's exactly the input the co-design process is meant to capture.
questions.professionalAnswer: My approach with skeptical team leads is never to lead with the policy, it's to lead with the bill they've already paid — the incident, the broken model, the three-week onboarding. Once that's visible, I pull one representative from each team into actually designing the standard rather than receiving it, because governance that teams co-own gets followed and governance that's handed down gets worked around. I keep version one narrow on purpose — naming and a testing floor, not a thirty-page document — pilot it somewhere willing, and let that team's story do the persuading for the next round. If a lead is still skeptical after seeing a real pilot result, that's a legitimate signal I need to understand their specific constraint better, not a reason to mandate compliance over their objection.
commonMistakes: Writes the governance standard unilaterally and presents it as a mandate rather than co-designing with team representatives
Tries to roll out a comprehensive standard across all six teams simultaneously instead of starting narrow with a pilot
Leads with the abstract value of governance instead of concrete, team-specific pain already experienced
Dismisses skepticism as resistance to change rather than investigating the specific constraint behind it
keyPoints: Uses concrete, already-experienced pain as the justification rather than abstract governance value
Co-designs the standard with team representatives rather than mandating it unilaterally
Starts narrow with a pilot team and uses that result as the adoption proof point
Treats persistent skepticism as a signal to investigate, not to override

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Grounds the pitch in concrete, team-specific pain rather than abstract value
Proposes co-design with team representatives rather than unilateral mandate
Proposes a narrow pilot-first rollout with a concrete proof point
Handles persistent skepticism constructively

questions.title: Leading a Migration From Legacy Stored-Procedure ETL to dbt
questions.prompt: Your company's core reporting pipeline is 200+ interdependent SQL stored procedures, written over a decade by people who've mostly left, and leadership has approved a migration to dbt — but the team maintaining those procedures is anxious about being asked to rebuild something they don't fully understand. As the lead, walk through how you'd run this migration.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd address the anxiety first, directly, because it's a legitimate reaction, not a morale problem to manage around: nobody fully understands 200 stored procedures built over a decade, and the plan has to acknowledge that rather than ask the team to pretend otherwise. Concretely, I'd start the migration with discovery, not rebuilding — running the existing procedures and capturing their actual output alongside the data lineage between them (which procedure reads from which, in what order), building a dependency map before writing a single dbt model, because that map is what lets the team migrate incrementally with confidence instead of guessing at hidden dependencies. I'd migrate the DAG from its sources forward, procedure by procedure or logical group by logical group, converting each to a dbt model and validating its output against the legacy procedure's output on the same inputs before considering that piece done — this gives the team an objective, low-stakes way to confirm they got each piece right rather than relying on memory of decade-old logic. I'd deliberately run the legacy and new systems in parallel for a meaningful window rather than cutting over immediately once each piece 'looks right,' since 'looks right' on a sample of recent data doesn't guarantee correctness on an edge case that only shows up once a quarter. Throughout, I'd frame this to the team as them becoming the people who finally understand this system, not as a test of what they already know.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd say to the team isn't about dbt at all — it's acknowledging that nobody, including whoever's left who touched these procedures longest, fully understands all 200 of them, and that's exactly why we're going to build a dependency map and validate output before we rebuild anything, not because we doubt them but because that's the only responsible way to migrate something this old. I'd have them lead the discovery phase, since they know this system better than anyone available, and frame each migrated piece as a validated win — legacy output matches new dbt output on real data — rather than a test they could fail. Running old and new in parallel for a while before full cutover is non-negotiable for me, because this is exactly the kind of system where a rare edge case hiding in a decade-old procedure is the thing that bites you three months after everyone thought it was done.
commonMistakes: Starts rebuilding in dbt immediately without first mapping dependencies and capturing legacy behavior
Treats the team's anxiety as a morale issue to manage rather than a legitimate signal about the system's real complexity
Cuts over from legacy to new before validating output on more than a quick sample
Frames the migration as testing what the team already knows rather than building shared understanding together
keyPoints: Validates the team's anxiety as reasonable given genuine system complexity, rather than dismissing it
Starts with dependency mapping and legacy output capture before rebuilding
Migrates and validates incrementally, comparing legacy vs. new output per piece
Runs legacy and new systems in parallel for a meaningful window before full cutover

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Validates the team's concern appropriately rather than dismissing it
Proposes dependency mapping/discovery before rebuilding
Proposes incremental migration with output validation per piece
Proposes a parallel-run period before full cutover

questions.title: Mentoring a Junior Engineer Through a Bad Snowflake Credit-Spend Incident
questions.prompt: A junior analytics engineer on your team accidentally left a large warehouse running at a high auto-suspend timeout over a long weekend, running up a significant, visible credit bill. They're clearly upset and worried about the consequences. Walk through how you'd handle this conversation and the aftermath.
questions.modelAnswer: My first move is separating the person from the system failure: a single engineer being able to accidentally cause a large, visible bill over a weekend with no automatic guardrail catching it is a gap in our resource-monitor coverage, not a personal failing serious enough to warrant the anxiety they're clearly feeling — and I'd say that to them directly and early, because a junior engineer spiraling about this helps nobody and isn't actually proportionate to what happened. I'd walk through what happened together calmly, not to assign blame but to understand the specific gap (was there no resource monitor on that warehouse? was the auto-suspend default misconfigured? was there no alerting on unusual weekend activity?), and I'd make a point of them being part of designing the fix, not just the subject of a post-mortem written about them. In reporting this up, I'd own it as a team-level gap in our safety nets, not lead with the individual's name, because that's both the more accurate framing and the one that keeps this person willing to take ownership of complex systems going forward instead of becoming overly cautious or afraid to work independently. The long-term fix is structural — resource monitors on every warehouse by default, alerting on anomalous weekend/off-hours usage — and I'd make sure leadership hears that the fix prevents this for everyone, not just for this one person going forward.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd say to them is: this is a gap in our guardrails, not a reflection on you, and I mean that literally — if a resource monitor had been in place, this wouldn't have been possible regardless of what warehouse setting got left on. I'd walk through what happened with them calmly and make them part of designing the fix, because turning this into something they helped solve is both the right way to build their confidence back and the right way to actually get buy-in on the resource-monitor rollout. When I report this up, I'm not leading with their name — I'm leading with 'here's the systemic gap, here's the fix, here's how it prevents this for every warehouse going forward,' because that's the accurate story and it's also the one that doesn't make this person afraid to touch Snowflake again.
commonMistakes: Frames the incident primarily as an individual mistake rather than a systemic guardrail gap
Escalates in a way that centers blame on the junior engineer rather than the missing resource-monitor coverage
Doesn't involve the engineer in designing the fix, treating them only as the subject of the incident
Fails to drive the structural fix (default resource monitors, anomaly alerting) to prevent recurrence for the whole team
keyPoints: Reframes the incident as a systemic guardrail gap rather than a personal failing
Handles the conversation with calm, blame-free fact-finding
Involves the engineer in designing the structural fix
Reports upward in a way that centers the systemic gap and fix, not the individual

Describes a calm, supportive, blame-free conversation approach
Involves the engineer in designing the structural fix
Reports upward accurately and proportionately

questions.title: Leading the Team Through a Cascading dbt Model Failure in Production
questions.prompt: A schema change upstream breaks a foundational staging model, which cascades to fail 60 downstream models overnight, and executive dashboards are showing stale or missing data by the time people log in. You're the lead on call. Walk through how you'd run the incident and the retrospective afterward.
questions.modelAnswer: First priority is stopping the bleeding and communicating, in that order, before root-causing: I'd check whether the failure is contained to dbt builds (meaning yesterday's good data is still sitting in the warehouse and 'stale' rather than 'wrong') versus something that actually corrupted data downstream, because that distinction determines whether this is urgent-but-not-dangerous or actually dangerous, and I'd communicate that distinction to stakeholders immediately — 'dashboards are showing yesterday's numbers, nothing is wrong with the data itself, we're fixing the pipeline' is a very different message than silence. I'd identify the single broken foundational model causing the cascade (dbt's own failure output typically makes this clear — one root failure with 60 downstream models skipped or failed as a result, not 61 independent failures) and focus entirely on fixing that one model first rather than getting pulled into triaging all 60 symptoms in parallel. Once the root model is fixed and a rerun is confirmed to flow through cleanly, I'd personally confirm a few of the highest-visibility executive dashboards are correct before declaring this resolved, rather than trusting the green dbt run alone. The retrospective afterward is where I'd push hardest: this cascade happened because 60 models depended on one model's shape without any contract catching a breaking change upstream — the real fix is enforcing contracts on foundational, heavily-depended-on models specifically, not just on cross-project public models, and I'd make sure that becomes a concrete action item with an owner and a date, not just a lesson learned in a document nobody revisits.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move in the incident itself is figuring out whether this is 'the dashboards are stale' or 'the dashboards are wrong,' because that changes both the urgency and the message I send out immediately — stakeholders can tolerate 'we're a few hours behind, nothing is incorrect' far better than silence while they wonder if a number they're about to present to a board is trustworthy. Then I go straight at the one root model dbt's failure output points to, not the 60 symptoms, and once it's fixed I personally spot-check a few of the exec-facing dashboards before I say we're done, because a green dbt run isn't the same as confirmed-correct to the people who actually look at the numbers. The retrospective is where this incident either turns into a real fix or just a story we tell later — I'd push hard for contracts on our foundational models specifically, since that's the actual gap that let one upstream change take down 60 models, and I'd want a named owner and a date on that action item, not a bullet point.
commonMistakes: Tries to triage all 60 downstream failures in parallel instead of identifying and fixing the single root model
Doesn't communicate proactively with stakeholders about the stale-vs-wrong distinction before they ask
Declares the incident resolved based on a green dbt run alone without spot-checking actual dashboard output
Lets the retrospective produce only a lesson-learned note without a concrete, owned action item (e.g., contracts on foundational models)
keyPoints: Distinguishes stale-but-correct data from actually-wrong data and communicates that distinction promptly
Identifies and fixes the single root cascading model rather than triaging all symptoms in parallel
Personally verifies real dashboard output before declaring resolution, not just a green pipeline run
Drives a concrete retrospective action item (e.g., contracts on foundational models) with an owner and date

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct incident triage: stale-vs-wrong distinction and proactive communication
Focuses on the single root model rather than all symptoms in parallel
Verifies real output before declaring resolution
Drives a concrete, owned retrospective action item
