questions.title: Negotiating a Single Definition of 'Revenue' Between Finance and Sales
questions.prompt: Finance defines 'revenue' as recognized revenue net of returns on an accrual basis; Sales defines it as booked deal value at signing, for commission purposes, and both have been using their own definition in dashboards for years. You've been asked to land one dbt-defined metric both teams will actually use. Walk through how you'd run this negotiation.
questions.modelAnswer: The first thing I'd establish, before proposing any single number, is that Finance's and Sales' definitions aren't actually in conflict about what 'revenue' means in the abstract — they're each correct answers to two different business questions (recognized accrual revenue for financial reporting; booked value for comp purposes), and trying to force both into one metric called 'revenue' is what caused the years-long disagreement in the first place. So the negotiation isn't 'whose definition wins,' it's getting both sides to agree these are two legitimately different, equally valid metrics that both deserve to exist with distinct, unambiguous names (e.g., net_recognized_revenue and booked_deal_value) rather than both teams' dashboards both labeling their own thing 'Revenue.' Once that reframe lands — which usually requires sitting both teams down together rather than shuttling between them, so neither side feels like I'm the one deciding their number is wrong — the actual technical work is straightforward: define both as separate dbt Semantic Layer metrics, each with its own clear label, and have both teams' dashboards pull from the Semantic Layer with the correctly-named metric rather than either team losing their number or being forced onto the other's. The win condition isn't 'one metric,' it's 'zero ambiguity about which metric is which,' and getting both sides to agree to that framing is the actual negotiation.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't walk into this trying to get one side to give up their number, because neither side is wrong — they're measuring genuinely different things for genuinely different purposes, and the real problem is both of those different things have been sharing the same label, 'revenue,' for years. My first move is getting both teams in the same room and naming that explicitly, because it reframes the conversation from a turf fight to a labeling problem, which is a much easier thing to agree on. Once they agree these are two distinct, legitimately necessary metrics, I define both clearly in the Semantic Layer with names that can't be confused for each other, and both teams keep their number — they just stop calling it the same thing as the other team's number.
commonMistakes: Tries to force both teams onto a single definition instead of recognizing they're measuring two legitimately different things
Negotiates with each team separately rather than bringing them together, which lets each side assume I'm taking the other's side
Treats this as purely a technical metric-definition problem without addressing the labeling/naming conflict first
Picks a winner based on seniority or political pressure rather than the underlying business validity of each definition
keyPoints: Recognizes both definitions as legitimately valid for different purposes, rather than one being 'wrong'
Reframes the conflict as a naming/labeling problem rather than a single-definition turf fight
Brings both teams together rather than negotiating with each separately
Resolves it technically by defining both as distinct, clearly-named Semantic Layer metrics

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recognizes both definitions as legitimately valid rather than forcing a single winner
Reframes the conflict as a naming/clarity problem
Proposes a joint (not separate) negotiation approach
Resolves it with a concrete, correct technical implementation (two distinct metrics)

questions.title: Making the Case for Analytics Engineering as Its Own Discipline
questions.prompt: A skeptical VP of Engineering thinks 'analytics engineering' is just a rebrand of BI developer or data analyst work and doesn't want to fund a distinct team or distinct hiring for it. Walk through how you'd make the case to them.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd avoid arguing about the label and instead point at a concrete gap in accountability that the VP can verify independently: ask who currently owns the correctness, testing, and documentation of the transformation logic sitting between raw data and every dashboard in the company — in most organizations without a defined analytics engineering function, the honest answer is 'nobody specifically,' because data engineers own getting data into the warehouse, data analysts/BI developers own building the dashboard on top, and the actual modeling layer in between — the joins, the business logic, the tested and documented marts — gets written ad hoc by whoever's building a given dashboard, with no consistent ownership, no tests, and no version control discipline applied to it as a first-class deliverable. I'd point to a specific real incident (a metric that disagreed across two dashboards, a broken report nobody could debug quickly because the transformation logic lived in an undocumented query) as the cost of that gap, and frame analytics engineering not as a rebrand but as the role that takes ownership of that specific unowned layer — with its own skill set (dbt, SQL at a software-engineering level of rigor, testing, CI/CD) that's genuinely distinct from both pipeline engineering and dashboard building. I'd propose starting small — reassigning one or two existing team members' time to this role rather than requesting net-new headcount immediately — and use a visible win (fixing the exact kind of incident I cited) as the evidence that earns the case for dedicated investment.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't fight about the title at all — I'd ask the VP directly: who owns the correctness of the SQL sitting between our raw tables and every dashboard in the company? In most places that haven't named this role, nobody actually does, and that's not a hypothetical, it's the thing behind the specific incident where two dashboards disagreed and it took days to figure out why. That gap, not the label, is my pitch — analytics engineering is the function that takes ownership of that layer with real engineering discipline, tests, version control, and I'd rather prove that with a small pilot using people we already have than ask for a budget line item up front and win the argument on paper instead of in practice.
commonMistakes: Argues about terminology/branding rather than pointing at a concrete, verifiable ownership gap
Doesn't tie the pitch to a specific real incident or cost the organization has already experienced
Asks for significant new headcount/budget upfront instead of proposing a small, low-risk pilot first
Describes analytics engineering only in terms of tools (dbt) rather than the ownership and discipline gap it fills
keyPoints: Points to a concrete, verifiable ownership gap (the modeling layer) rather than arguing about labels
Grounds the case in a specific real incident or cost already experienced by the organization
Proposes a small pilot with existing people rather than requesting upfront headcount
Frames the discipline in terms of ownership and rigor, not just tooling

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Avoids a label/terminology argument, focuses on a concrete gap
Grounds the case in a specific, real, verifiable incident or cost
Proposes a low-risk pilot approach rather than an upfront ask
Clearly articulates the ownership/discipline distinction from adjacent roles

questions.title: Handling a Senior Analyst Who Resists dbt Testing Discipline
questions.prompt: A senior analyst on your team, experienced but new to dbt, keeps shipping models without tests or documentation, saying it 'slows them down' and that they've 'never needed tests before.' Deadlines are real, and they're otherwise a strong contributor. Walk through how you'd handle this.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd start by taking the 'slows me down' objection seriously rather than dismissing it as resistance to good practice, because it's often true in the narrow, immediate sense — writing a not_null and unique test does add a few minutes to shipping a model — and arguing against that fact doesn't land. Instead I'd make the tradeoff concrete and specific to something that's already happened or is likely to: find or construct a real example of an untested model from this person's own work that broke silently downstream, and walk through how long it took to find and fix versus how long a basic test would have taken to write, so the cost comparison is specific and credible rather than a generic 'testing is good practice' lecture. I'd also separate the two asks — tests and documentation — since they have different cost/benefit profiles; a minimal test suite (not_null, unique, relationships on key columns) is a very small time cost for a large downstream-debugging-time savings, while documentation is more of a team-communication investment, and I'd negotiate a realistic minimum bar for each rather than demanding the maximum on both. If the behavior continues after a genuine, two-way conversation and an agreed minimum standard, I'd treat it as a performance conversation rather than a technical one, because at that point it's not about convincing them tests have value, it's about whether they're willing to follow a team standard that's been fairly negotiated.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't open with 'tests are a best practice' because that's not actually in dispute for someone experienced — I'd open with a specific example, ideally from their own recent work, of something that broke silently and cost real debugging time, and let that example make the argument instead of me lecturing. I'd also split the ask: a minimal test bar (not_null, unique, relationships on the columns that actually matter) is genuinely cheap and I'd hold firm on that; documentation I'd treat as more negotiable on scope and timeline. If after a real conversation and an agreed minimum they're still skipping it, that's no longer a 'let me convince you' problem, that's a 'this is the team standard, I need you to follow it' conversation, and I'd have it as directly and respectfully as that framing requires.
commonMistakes: Argues abstractly for the value of testing instead of grounding the conversation in a specific, credible example
Treats testing and documentation as one undifferentiated ask instead of negotiating a realistic minimum for each separately
Avoids escalating to a performance conversation even after a fair standard has been set and repeatedly not followed
Dismisses the 'slows me down' objection instead of acknowledging its narrow truth before making the larger cost-benefit case
keyPoints: Acknowledges the narrow truth in the 'slows me down' objection before making the broader case
Grounds the argument in a specific, credible example rather than a generic lecture on best practices
Separates testing and documentation asks, negotiating a realistic minimum bar for each
Escalates to a performance conversation if a fairly-negotiated standard continues to be ignored

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Acknowledges the objection's narrow validity before countering it
Uses a specific, credible example rather than a generic argument
Negotiates a realistic, separated minimum standard for tests vs. documentation
Appropriately escalates to a performance conversation if needed

questions.title: Telling a Stakeholder No on a Sub-Minute Snowflake Refresh Request
questions.prompt: A VP of Sales wants their pipeline dashboard refreshing every 30 seconds from Snowflake, believing it will help reps close deals faster. Given your platform's current dbt-on-a-schedule architecture, this isn't realistic without a significant, costly redesign. Walk through how you'd handle this conversation.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd start by understanding the actual underlying need rather than taking '30-second refresh' as the literal requirement, because in my experience that kind of specific number usually stands in for a real but different frustration — most likely that reps are making decisions on data that feels too stale relative to how fast deals move, not that they're staring at the dashboard waiting for a number to tick over in real time. Once I understand that, I'd be direct about the actual tradeoff: our current architecture refreshes on a schedule, and getting to true 30-second freshness would mean a fundamentally different (and meaningfully more expensive, both in engineering effort and ongoing Snowflake compute cost) streaming architecture, which I can scope honestly but shouldn't promise casually. I'd then offer the realistic middle options: a meaningfully shorter scheduled refresh (e.g., every 5-15 minutes) if that actually solves the real staleness concern, or if genuine near-real-time visibility into specific high-value deal events matters, a narrower, targeted streaming solution for just that specific signal rather than a wholesale rebuild of the whole dashboard's refresh architecture. The goal is giving the VP a real choice with real tradeoffs stated honestly, not a flat no with no alternative, and not a vague 'we'll look into it' that avoids the conversation.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first question back to the VP, genuinely, is what decision are reps making differently with 30-second data that they can't make with 10-minute data — because usually there's a real frustration under the specific number, and it's not actually 'I need to watch a counter in real time.' Once I understand that, I'm honest about the tradeoff: true 30-second freshness is a different architecture, not a config change, and it has a real cost I can scope but won't hand-wave. Then I offer real alternatives — a much shorter scheduled refresh if that's actually enough, or a narrow streaming solution for the one specific signal that genuinely needs to be near-real-time, rather than rebuilding everything. I want them to leave the conversation with an actual choice, not a no and not an open-ended promise.
commonMistakes: Takes the specific '30 seconds' request literally without probing the underlying business need behind it
Gives a flat no without offering any realistic alternative
Agrees to scope a full streaming redesign without being upfront about its real cost and effort
Avoids giving a direct answer, leaving the stakeholder with an open-ended 'we'll see' instead of real options
keyPoints: Probes the underlying business need behind the specific refresh-rate request
Is honest and specific about the real architectural and cost tradeoff of true near-real-time refresh
Offers concrete realistic alternatives (shorter schedule, or narrow targeted streaming) rather than a flat no
Leaves the stakeholder with an actual informed choice rather than a vague deferral

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Probes the real underlying need rather than taking the literal number at face value
Gives an honest, specific explanation of the real tradeoff/cost
Offers concrete, realistic alternatives
Professional, direct communication that avoids both a flat no and a vague deferral

questions.title: Resolving a Mesh Ownership Conflict Between Two Teams
questions.prompt: Since adopting dbt Mesh, Marketing and Product both believe they should own a widely-used public model, customer_lifecycle_stage, and the disagreement has stalled a needed change to it for three weeks. Both have legitimate claims: Marketing created it originally, Product now consumes and modifies it most. As the platform lead, walk through how you resolve this.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd resist picking a winner based on who created the model first, since original authorship is a weak proxy for who should actually own long-term correctness and evolution of a model three weeks into an active stall — the better criterion is which team is best positioned to be accountable for the model's correctness going forward, which usually tracks closer to who understands and most frequently needs to change its logic, in this case arguably Product. Rather than unilaterally deciding, I'd bring both teams together and make the ownership criteria explicit and agreed-upon before applying them to this specific case: who has the domain expertise to validate changes are correct, who's paged if it breaks, who has capacity to review change requests from the other team promptly. Once criteria are agreed, applying them to this case becomes much less personal than 'I chose Product over Marketing.' Critically, ownership of a public model doesn't mean the other team loses access or input — Marketing keeps consuming it via cross-project ref() and can propose changes through a request process, they just stop being the ones who merge changes to it directly. I'd document this decision and the criteria used, both so future ownership disputes have a precedent to point to, and so the losing team can see the decision was principled, not political.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't let this stay stalled on 'who made it first,' because that's not actually the right question three weeks in — I'd get both teams in a room and agree on ownership criteria first, independent of this specific case: who has the expertise to validate changes, who's on call for it, who can turn around review requests quickly. Then we apply those criteria to this model, which in this case likely points to Product given they're the heavier, more frequent consumer and modifier. I'd be explicit that owning the model doesn't cut Marketing out — they still consume it and can request changes, they just aren't the ones merging to it going forward. And I'd write the decision and the criteria down, because the next ownership dispute shouldn't start from zero.
commonMistakes: Picks the owner based on original authorship rather than who's best positioned for ongoing accountability
Decides unilaterally without agreeing on criteria with both teams first, making the decision feel political rather than principled
Treats 'losing' ownership as losing access entirely, rather than preserving the other team's consumption and change-request rights
Doesn't document the decision or criteria, leaving the next similar dispute to start from scratch
keyPoints: Uses ongoing accountability/capability as the ownership criterion rather than original authorship
Agrees on explicit ownership criteria with both teams before applying them to the specific case
Clarifies that losing ownership doesn't mean losing consumption or change-request ability
Documents the decision and criteria as precedent for future disputes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Uses a sound, accountability-based ownership criterion rather than authorship
Proposes agreeing on criteria jointly before applying them
Clarifies the non-owning team retains consumption/change-request rights
Documents the decision as precedent
